name: CLERESTORY INC
mission: AS WITH NATURAL DISASTERS THERE ARE STAGES TO THE COMPLETE RECOVERY OF A COMMUNITY. THESE INCLUDE: SEARCH AND RESCUE, RELIEF EFFORTS, REBUILDING AND RESTORATION. SIMILAR TO NATURAL DISASTERS, THERE ARE STAGES IN ADMINISTERING AID TO THOSE EXPERIENCING DISASTERS IN THEIR PERSONAL LIVES. WE ARE THANKFUL FOR AGENCIES/ORGANIZATIONS/CHURCHES THAT PROVIDE RELIEF IN MINISTERING TO INDIVIDUALS, BUT SO MANY TIMES THE HELP IS TEMPORARY FOR EXAMPLE FEEDING THE HUNGRY, PROVIDING CLOTHING, PAYING OVER-DUES BILLS, ETC. name: BIG HOUSE TEXAS CO ST MARKS UMC
mission: BIGHOUSE TEXAS, Inc.("BIG HOUSE") is a religious work camp for Jr. High Youth (6-8th grades)who work to repair and repaint needful churches and social agencies. BIG HOUSE is an acronym, which stands for Believing in God and Helping Others Understand through Service Everywhere. Most churches that will benefit from the work camps are housed in older, historic buildings with aging congregations who cannot afford to pay someone to maintain the buildings or do the necessary repairs themselves.In 1996, a couple of youth directors got together and brought their Jr. High youth to do a mission work camp in Athens, Texas. There were only 25 people in this camp, but together they worked on Mt. Selman United Methodist Church. This became a special project of the United Methodist Church, and it has continued to grow, as volunteers have come together to make it what it is every year. The work camps involve religious, educational, and charitable activities. Charitable projects done by BIG HOUSE work camps include, but are not limited to the following; painting churches, building wheelchair ramps, landscaping, repairing handrails, preparing meals, stocking food at a food pantry, and otherwise assisting church members.The work camps also emphasize spiritual growth, and educational opportunities. The children participate in daily devotionals and worship services. Each morning before anything else has begun, the youth and adults meet for a morning devotion to get the day started. They have a lunch devotional at the work site, sometimes shared with the client. There is an evening worship service for all involved. Educating these youth on the principle of responsibility is another component of the work camps. Responsibility is not just to their home church, but to the church as a whole, and to their community not just at home, but to the world. The lessons learned at these camps is helping to develop servant leaders, and grow them in a way that they will better their world. Camp Materials are the largest expenses incurred at camp, this includes all materials used to build, paint, and repair the homes that are worked on.

name: RRV FORUM GROUP INC
mission: RUSSIAN RIVER VALLEY (RRV) PINOT FORUM: One of the organizations means of implementing its goals is through the holding of an annual meeting and seminar for invited influential wine professionals. This activity, which is an outgrowth of a similar educational event pioneered by a group of RRV wineries prior to the formation of this entity, is known as The Pinot Forum, after the major grape varietal grown in the RRV American Viticultural Area (AVA); Pinot Noir. The AnnuualPinot Forum was held in August. Influential wine directors and sommeliers from around the country were invited to participate. In a three day period, several educational events were held that included explanation of the unique climate, geology and growing conditions of the RRV, including the nature of its subregions, tours of vineyards in the subregions of the RRV AVA, tasting of wines from the subregions, and food and wine pairings that accentuated the value of Pinot Noir to the food industry. A compendium of data about the RRV AVA was prepared and given to the attendees as a study guide. This educational seminar benefits the attendees, the consumers that patronize their establishments and, indirectly, the wineries that produce wines from the RRV AVA, as well as the many grape growers in this region.

name: PLANT-BASED PREVENTION OF DISEASE INC
mission: Our Section 501(c)(3) recognized nonprofit Plant-based Prevention Of Disease, Inc. produces an annual conference focused upon the health professions, in the month of May. Our 2017 event brought together 168 individuals: 107 paid registrants, 33 speakers, 3 other board members and regular staff, and about 25 volunteers. Conmtinuing education credits were awarded to physicians, osteopaths, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, registered nurses, registered dietitians, physical therapists, acupuncturists, psychologists, CHES certified health educators, and NASM certified personal trainers.Our specific program efforts and intentions for the May 2017 conference were detailed in our PRESS RELEASE:BEGINRecognized experts in medicine, nutrition and behavior change gather to share evidence on best practices to prevent disease May 18 to 20, 2017 at the 4th annual national Plant-based Prevention Of Disease (P-POD) conference at the University of New Mexico, Albuquerque.According to the Centers for Disease Control, 86% of U.S. health care expenditures are attributed to chronic disease, 7 of the 10 leading causes of death are chronic diseases, and half of American adults suffer from at least one. Yet, many of these diseases are preventable through dietary and lifestyle changes, which could save millions of lives and billions of dollars, and improve quality of life immeasurably.Plant-based whole foods have long been associated with improved biomarkers of health, and those following vegetarian diets show lower rates of nearly every chronic disease.Healthcare providers can be on the forefront of saving lives by promoting dietary changes, yet many are unfamiliar with the substantial scientific data on disease prevention, and untrained in behavior change methods. The P-POD conference, a nonprofit without commercial funding, brings together 33 distinguished speakers to discuss nutritional research and action against disease, via lectures and round tables.A new 2017 conference collaborator is the Navajo Nation, apparently the first governmental entity in the U.S. to implement a sales tax on junk food, while eliminating taxes on fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds, beans and water. Its 2015 proclamation recognizing National Diabetes Awareness Month included recommendations that the Din (Navajo) people eat more plant-based meals, and Vice President Jonathan Nez is following up by offering opening remarks at P-POD 2017, after hosting and leading (with ultra-running champion Scott Jurek) a pre-conference 5K run.P-POD 2017 also commemorates the 25th anniversary of major nonprofit co-sponsor Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine (PCRM) launching the "New 4 Food Groups" (vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes) as the foundation of diets that reduce our population's risk of preventable diseases. PCRMs Neal Barnard, MD was joined in this 1992 announcement by Denis Burkitt, MD and T. Colin Campbell, PhD. Dr. Burkitt, then in his final year of life, had made ground-breaking research discoveries that fiber, the most distinct marker for plant-derived whole foods, was associated with reduced risk of several chronic diseases such as colon cancer. Shortly before this, the New York Times had proclaimed the striking first results from Dr. Campbell's now-widely-renowned "China study" research. In celebration of all this, 2017s keynote address, named the First Annual Denis Burkitt Memorial Lecture, will be delivered by Dr. Campbell, who also founded nonprofit co-sponsor T. Colin Campbell Center for Nutrition Studies. Some of the other presenters: Brenda Davis, RD; Milton Mills, MD; Lois Ellen Frank, PhD; Michael Klaper, MD; Caroline Trapp, DNP.Up to 17.5 hours of continuing education credits are offered to numerous types of health professionals. P-POD is committed to affordable registration costs. The public is welcome and sizable student discounts are available.P-PODs 2017 Theme is: Evidence-Based Nutrition for the Entire Health Care Team.Reclaiming Simple Traditional Plant-based Foods in the Prevention / Treatment of Diabetes and Other Chronic Diseases. Additional nonprofit co-sponsors and collaborators include Vegetarian Nutrition Dietetic Practice Group, University of New Mexico Section of Integrative Medicine and Center for Life, New Mexico Nurses Association, Dietitians in Integrative and Functional Medicine, Institute of American Indian Arts, and Asian Indians in Nutrition and Dietetics.ENDNoted above, a new strong emphasis for THIS particular year was the health and chronic disease risk vulnerabilities of Native American populations in general, and of the southwestern Navajo Nation in particular. The following, based on an article by our board member Kathy Pollard MS, shows in detail this context for our 2017 efforts to advance public health purposes accordingly:BEGINIt is tragic to witness the continued rise in chronic disease rates around the globe, particularly for diabetes and the commonly accompanied cardiovascular disease. Much of this suffering is due to changes away from the various age-old health-supporting diets, based primarily on local plant foods, consumed by indigenous communities worldwide. We have for example seen diabetes rates soar across Native American communities, such as the Pima tribe of Arizona, showing one of the worlds highest rates of diabetes, accompanied by obesity and hypertension. Some may assume a genetic cause, but although genetic makeup may allow for a tendency or susceptibility toward a particular disease, we know that environmental factors are what allow genes to express themselves via active disease.Interestingly, those of the Pima tribe living across the border in Mexico do not suffer from high rates of diabetes. Whats different? They share similar genetic makeup but a very different lifestyle from Pima in Arizona, where the diet strays from their native foods of beans, maize, wheat, squash, and many indigenous plants including wild spinach, mesquite pods, cholla buds, and possibly some wild game and fish. Arizona Pima mainly eat cheap fast food and processed animal products, and are much less active physically than their Mexican cousins, and all of this helps promote obesity and insulin resistance. Diabetes risk differences among Pima suggest that devastating chronic diseases may be prevented in communities, as well as overcome, through lifestyle changes which hold more promise than merely medical treatment in response to symptoms. For several generations, many tribal members in the southwest and elsewhere have depended largely on commodity foods provided by the federal government, including canned meat, cheese, powdered milk and other highly processed foods, and throughout this timespan we have indeed seen diabetes rates increase dramatically among them.Fortunately there are organizations and healthcare practitioners working within communities to change the trajectory of such disease epidemics. One is Caroline Trapp, DNP, APN-BC, CDE, FAANP, nurse practitioner and director of diabetes education and care for the Physicians Committee for Responsible Medicine (PCRM). She explains, Diabetes and the complications of uncontrolled diabetes are epidemic in New Mexico, and have especially impacted Native American communities. Native American teens are the fastest growing demographic group in terms of the number of people developing the disease. Ive seen both the devastation caused by the failure of conventional approaches, and the powerful benefits when people who are at risk for, or who have diabetes, shift to a plant-based dietary pattern.Dr. Trapp has spearheaded a project offering much needed education to healthcare workers and leaders in and around the Native American communities of the Southwest, and now introducing the Plant-based Prevention of Disease (P-POD) conference to Albuquerque, New Mexico in May 2017. This conference, partly inspired by the work and research of keynote speaker T. Colin Campbell, PhD on the power of traditional plant-based foods to overcome chronic disease, and founded by Bob LeRoy, MS EdM RD, brings together experts in the field of lifestyle medicine and plant-based nutrition to educate those on the frontlines of addressing diabetes and related diseases. both healthcare practitioners and the public.Dr. Trapp was also involved with another program illustrating the effects of cultural shifts away from native foods: the Marshall Island Diabetes Intervention Project, led by Brenda Davis RD, who will also be a speaker at this years P-POD conference. Type 2 diabetes is the number one cause of death and disability in this island nation, where most individuals have it or else develop pre-diabetes by the time they are adults, though most dont know they have the disease and dont get treated until severe effects like circulatory or kidney damage occur. According to recent studies, the economic benefit of EV grid integration could be as high as $1000 - $2000 per vehicle per year which is sufficient to eliminate the incremental cost difference between EVs and conventional gas-powered vehicles. However, it is essential that the consumer, rather than utilities and auto companies, gain the great majority of this economic benefit. If this does not occur, then EV adoption and EV-grid integration will be too slow to have a significant impact on reducing greenhouse gas emissions and mitigating the global climate crisis.

name: CHOLESTEROL GENETICS AND HEART DISEASE INSTITUTE
mission: 2016 ActivitiesScientific PresentationsSuperko HR, Garrett B, Reade S, Panholzer G, Snyder C, Schaefer E. Firefighters on the East and West Coasts have Increased CHD Risk Associated with Insulin Resistance and Small LDL. National Lipid Association annual scientific meeting Orlando, Florida 2016.Firefighter Heart Disease Prevention ActivitiesIn 2016 the CGHDI held multiple meetings with members of the Monterey Fire Department to complete the screening of the entire department for subclinical and clinical coronary heart disease that was started in 2015. Data analysis included an executive summary report that was shared with the fire chief and department.Discussions were held with Dr. Arthur Agatston n regard to incorporating his successful South Beach Diet into the Firefighter Heart disease screening program. The South Beach Diet is essentially a Mediterranean diet that is now considered to be the best diet in regard to general heart disease prevention.Community lectures were held to explain the high risk of heart disease in firefighters and the role of noninvasive imaging and advanced blood tests in identifying the firefighters vulnerable to a coronary heart disease event.Discussions were held at the American College of Cardiology annual scientific meeting April 2-5 in regard to the CGHDI efforts on behalf of firefighters.A meeting held at the Nebrasks Heart Institute in October 2016 explained the details of conducting fire department heart disease screening and early implementation was initiated by Nebraska Heart Institute based on the materials and information supplied by the CGHDI.Discussions were held with Boston HeartDx in regard to supporting a National Firefighter Heart Disease screening program by providing access to sophisticated blood tests at research pricing and allow a wider reach for screening programs based on the CGHDI efforts and materials but conducted by local medical advocates.The Seaside Fire department was contacted and following a series of meetings with the fire chief and his lieutenant, the department was screened over a 4-month period in 2016 and extending into 2017. Debriefing meetings were held to discuss the general (deidentified) results as well as individual discussions with firefighters who revealed a high-risk status based on the blood and imaging tests.As part of the program, expenses were incurred for the noninvasive heart CT scan tests obtained at local imaging facilities.A Trifold firefighter heart disease document was created specifically for the Seaside fire department. Powerpoint slide presentations were updated and presented at several lay and professional lectures. Web siteThe web site was updated with special reference to the Monterey and Seaside firefighter screening. Various updates were included.OtherParticipation in SHAPE (Society for Heart Attack Prevention and Eradication) activities continued. A primary focus was creating a grant addressing improved CHD risk determination utilizing noninvasive imaging. Activities included participation in lectures during the annual board meeting that highlighted the firefighter heart disease problem.2017 GoalsExplore the potential to screen the Salinas Fire service for subclinical CHD and metabolic/genetic disorders linked to CHD risk.Describe and explain the purpose of the Firefighter Heart Disease screening program to interested medical groups and fire departmemnts.Explore expansion of the Firefighter Heart Disease Prevention program to sites across the USA.Enhance web site presence and functionality.Analyze screening program data.Submit and present analysis of the data at scientific/medical meetings.

name: EMERGING LEADERS INITIATIVE NFP
mission: OVERALL CONTEXT: By stewarding the significant contributions from volunteers, including mentors and committee members, ELI's primary financial investment was the time of the Executive Director committed to leading the program, coordinating volunteers, and evaluating the quality of experience and outcomes. Leveraging many diverse and committed volunteers, ELI was able to serve at a level well above the capacity of one full-time employee and maximize the generosity and partnership of donors. Given this framework, we have outlined the following three areas to show how the Executive Directors time and donor dollars are allocated. 1. PROGRAM DELIVERY (~65% of Executive Director time): The ELI program is executed and sustained by one full-time employee, the Executive Director, with the collaborative and substantial support of volunteers and the Board of Directors. The Executive Director is responsible for leading, coordinating, and evaluating the three primary aspects of program delivery in 2017-2018: 1. Mentor Development and Support The training, development, and support of 16 volunteer mentors during the FY18 program year. This involved, but was not limited to, regular 1:1 in-person and video coaching meetings, bi-weekly video training calls, weekly communication, and mentoring support. 2. Mentee Development and Support - The training, development, and support of 38 mentees during the FY18 program year, including creating and revising 12 unique online lessons, in-person and video coaching sessions, and weekly communication. 3. Technology, Communication, and Administrative Management - The development and management of ELIs online presence, logistics, and all other technology systems related to operating the ELI program. To effectively administer our program within its scalable model, the Executive Director created, coordinated, and managed ELI's specific utilization of Google Office Suite, online content platform, Pathwright, and the video platform, Zoom. Each mentor had a Zoom and Pathwright account which allowed groups to connect consistently, regardless of location. This model also presented the opportunity to expand beyond Chicago or a centralized location to help more emerging leaders discover Gods design for their lives. Over the first two years, ELI has served individuals in seven states. Last year, 96% of mentors and mentees surveyed had a significant breakthrough and found the ELI experience personally transformative.; 2. RECRUITMENT & OUTREACH (~25% of Executive Director time): Aligned with its mission to help emerging leaders discover Gods design, the Executive Director and many volunteers committed time to connect with and outreach to new mentors and mentees. With a collaborative spirit, the Executive Director and volunteers engaged with other organizations, churches, and companies who share their passion to provide this mentoring opportunity to others. This past year, the Executive Director coordinated an investment in professional videos to help share more stories of program impact and provide examples of how God has transformed the lives of mentors and mentees. With the support of volunteers, the Executive Director led the planning and execution of ELIs second annual fundraising event which helped to raise 75% of ELIs yearly budget as well as to recruit new mentors and mentees. As a result of these collective outreach efforts, ELI has grown each year, from 37 total mentors and mentees in 2016-2017 to 54 total mentors and mentees in 2017-2018 to 75 total mentors and mentees for 2018-2019.; 3. COMMUNITY FORMATION (~10% of Executive Director time): Community is essential as ELI members seek to seek to model Christs leadership in and through their work. 96% of participants found that their peers helped them to grow as a Christ-centered leader and experience mentor groups that were trusting and transparent. In response to a growing number of ELI alumni, the Executive Director and volunteers helped to create additional opportunities for connection and growth this past year. For example, monthly lunches and bi-weekly equipping calls were set up to increase the ways that mentors and mentees within the ELI community could connect. The Executive Director planned both a Kick-Off Event and a Capstone event where alumni mentors and mentees were able to connect with current mentors and mentees in meaningful ways. In addition, serving roles and teams were established as ways for alumni to serve others, including a social, finance, communications, recruitment, and training team. With over 15 alumni volunteers serving on ELI teams this past year, many new opportunities were available to support and grow the community. The continual stewardship and increase in volunteer contributions also led to the capacity to create a second mentoring experience for ELI alumni which began in fall 2018-2019, The ELI Builder Mastermind. The Builder Mastermind will serve 12 ELI alumni by providing a consistent environment for them to continue to grow their pursuit of God's purpose for them in work within a supportive, Christ-centered community.

name: ASHEVILLE MOVEMENT COMMUNITY INC
mission: Asheville Movement Community, Inc. during 2017 hosted three weekly free-form movement events in service to an economically and socially diverse local community. Each event included a review of the organization's event guidelines, in order to encourage participation through self-expression and safe free-form movement. Participants ranged from children under supervision of their parents to persons aged 75 and older, and efforts were made so that, if possible, those coping with particular physical limitations might feel welcome to attend. All in all, our regularly scheduled events served about 7,159 attendees this year.Volunteers and elected participants continued to refine the organizations personnel and governance infrastructure, both to create opportunities for participation and to preserve the system of checks and balances. This was also done with an eye to reducing excessive administrative overhead, and improving the experience of community members who are not organizers, by shifting the format of the open community gatherings to be more connection- and feedback-focused than governance-focused. Pathways remain for direct participation in organizational decision making. AMC hosted four Dancers Gatherings (including the Annual Meeting) to help engage the community in the volunteerism and organizational decision making, and to open a more personal pathway to feedback with the community. Several volunteers were trained to hold leadership positions, such as Room Coordinators, in the organization.The Annual Community Meeting (third annual, and a Dancers Gathering) was held in November. Participants were invited to dialogue about several topics related to the organization's growth and development, including: childcare at events, how to elicit participation, policy, thriving, how to improve AMCs offerings, and our long term vision. Participants were also provided with current information about the organization's finances, staff and operation s. It is estimated that well over 1,000 volunteer hours were contributed to the mission and events in 2017. AMC also continued to train new officers and individual volunteers in operational tasks including budgeting and finance reporting, governance process and event production. In 2017 AMC brought on one new volunteer coordinator. The part-time Interim Executive Director and part-time Interim Executive Secretary positions were made permanent. The part-time Event Coordinator position was reinstated in November.AMC moved its primary events in May 2017 to a new venue that offered lower rental fees and a more welcoming environment. Attendance was impacted just after the move, yet was stabilized by the end of the year, as many new dance participants became regulars. AMC has been able to maintain an uninterrupted event schedule while continuing to offer affordable sliding scale admission prices for dancers.2017 exhibited a marked increase of extra-organizational collaborations with past AMC movement event facilitators, and with other new facilitators drawn from within our own dance community or from similar modalities active in the external community. There were seven live music events which have opened the door for similar collaborations, four collaborations with another freeform movement organization in the area, one involving a group from Oregon on a dance bus tour, and seven other guest facilitations. AMC pursued these collaborations while also offering guidance and support for the guest facilitators and musicians in creating appropriate settings for the free-form dance experience and safe authentic expression. AMC and Warren Wilson College Wellness Department entered a Memorandum of Understanding to get students involved in our movement practice. Four times annually AMC utilizes a venue at the college where students may engage as volunteers and are invited to participate in the dance event for free. Another collaboration with the Asheville Massage School offered participants an introduction to the practice by one of our facilitators. In 2017, AMC also collaborated with another 501(c)(3) nonprofit, Our VOICE, to raise over $1,000 in funds and externally donated supplies for their cause.

Once subsistence fishing is no longer necessary however, they are unaware of the need to and ways to release fish alive. Our Best Practices focuses on education and access.; DECOMMISSIONING - Some of oil rigs in the Santa Barbara Channel are reaching the end of their useful life. California law provides for that each platform can be evaluated to determine whether partial or total removal results in the highest net environmental benefit but unfortunately does not create a workable process to do so. The platforms provide a rich environment for aquatic life. Cost savings in the case of partial removal would in part establish an endowment for the ocean to fund research. The Sportfishing Conservancy has educated other parties interested in the marine environment to the benefits of partial removal and supported proposed changes to the law to make this doable.; NO MOTOR TOURNAMENT - The No Motor Tournament is held annually in Carpinteria in conjunction with United Anglers. All forms of fishing are okay as long as done using human power [i.e. no motor boats]. The winner is determined by total length of legal fish caught and released. The tournament highlights the importance of the Carpinteria Salt Marsh in providing a nursery for marine species with proceeds donated to The Land Trust of Santa Barbara County. mission: FACULTY, FACILITIES AND CAPITAL EQUIPMENT: IN 2017, THE FOUNDATION PROVIDED 25,000 TO SUPPORT THE COE DEAN'S FUNDS FOR "EXCELLENCE IN RESEARCH AWARDS" TO OUTSTANDING FACULTY AND STAFF. THIS CONTINUES THE HISTORY OF FOUNDATION GRANTS TO BENEFIT FACULTY AND CAPITAL PROJECTS: A NEW STUDENT ACTIVITY VAN IN 2015 (28,812); COE FACILITIES IMPROVEMENT 50/50 DRIVE IN 2014 (23,302); AND LIBRARY STUDY ROOM IN 2011 (10,000).; DEPARTMENTS, SCHOLARSHIPS & STUDENT ACTIVIIES: IN 2017, FOUR DONOR-DESIGNATED STUDENT SCHOLARSHIP CONTRIBUTIONS WERE TRANSFERRED TO THE ENGINEERING SCHOOL RANGING FROM 250 TO 15,000. IN ADDITION, THREE DONATIONS (FROM 100 TO 5,000) FOR DESIGNATED DEPARTMENTAL FUNDING WERE EITHER TRANSFERRED TO THE COE OR PLACED IN A FOUNDATION- RESERVED ACCOUNT FOR THAT DEPARTMENT'S FUTURE USE (THIRD ACCOMPLISHMENT). FROM THE FOUNDATION'S 2010 INCEPTION TO YEAR-END 2017, 231,742 IN RESTRICTED OR DESIGNATED DONATIONS HAVE BEEN RECEIVED AND HAVE BEEN TRANSFERRED TO THE COLLEGE. THE MAJORITY OF THESE DESIGNATED DONATIONS GO TOWARDS SPECIFIC SCHOLARSHIPS, INCLUDING A SCHOLARSHIP FUNDRAISING CAMPAIGN BY THE FOUNDATION IN 2012 WHICH RAISED ALMOST 32,000. OTHERS HAVE GONE TO SPECIFIED COE CAUSES LIKE ENDOWED CHAIRS AND FELLOWSHIPS. RESTRICTED CONTRIBUTIONS ARE ALSO PROVIDED FOR DONOR-SPECIFIED DEPARTMENTAL DISCRETIONARY USE, LIKE FACULTY OR ALUMNI RECOGNITION AWARDS, STUDENT CLUB ACTIVITIES OR DEPARTMENTAL EXPENSES. MATCHING FUNDS RECEIVED FROM DONORS EMPLOYERS ARE RESTRICTED TO THE SAME DESIGNATION AS THE DONOR SPECIFIED.; COE, DEPARTMENTAL RESERVED FUNDS: IN 2017, SINCE ITS INCEPTION, THE FOUNDATION HAS RESERVED A POOL OF FUNDS FOR THE DEAN'S DISCRETION FOR EXPENSES NOT WITHIN THE COE'S RESTRICTED BUDGET (E.G. 2016 STRATEGIC PLAN) AND ANOTHER POOL FOR DEPARTMENTS THAT PREFER DIRECT PAYMENTS FOR NON-BUDGET EXPENSES. IN 2017 THE FOUNDATION MADE ONE GRANT FROM THOSE RESERVES FOR THE COE DEANS DISCRETIONARY EXPENSES AND A SECOND GRANT FOR CHEMICAL ENGINEERING ACADEMY EXPENSES. TO DATE, INVOICES TOTALING 71,343 HAVE BEEN PAID ON BEHALF OF THE DEAN AND CHEMICAL ENGINEERING DEPARTMENT. AT YEAR-END 2017, THE FOUNDATION MAINTAINS 50,831 ON ITS BALANCE SHEET RESTRICTED FOR THE DIRECTIVES OF THE DEAN AND CHEMICAL ENGINEERING DEPARTMENT.; OTHER: AT YEAR-END 2017, THE FOUNDATION HELD 82,086 IN ENDOWED FUNDS AND USES THE MISSOURI ENDOWMENT POOL TO INVEST ITS FUNDS UNDER AN AGENCY AGREEMENT. THE DISTRIBUTIONS FROM THAT ENDOWMENT ACCOUNT ARE COLLECTED AND USED FOR COOPERATIVE PROJECTS WITH THE COE. IN 2017, THE VALUE OF THE ENDOWMENT INCREASED 9,300 OR 9.4% AND A PORTION OF THE DISTRIBUTION EARNINGS WERE SPENT TO COVER THE EXPENSES OF THE 2017 FOUNDATION FUNDRAISING CAMPAIGN.

name: NORTHERN YOUTH PROJECT
mission: NORTHERN YOUTH PROJECT HAD A SUCCESSFUL, DYNAMIC YEAR OF PROGRAMMING MENTORING YOUTH THROUGH LEADERSHIP IN ARTS AND AGRICULTURAL. MAJOR ACCOMPLISHMENTS INCLUDE THE COMPLETION OF THE "FOR THE LOVE OF LAND" ARTS PROGRAM WHERE TWO SCULPTURES WERE CREATED FROM TRASH CLEANED FROM THREE REGIONAL ACEQUIAS OR WATERWAYS. THE SCULPTURES SHOWED HOW TRASH COULD BE TRANSFORMED INTO TREASURE. THE SCULPTURES WERE CELEBRATED AT A COMMUNITY ARTS OPENING IN ESPANOLA, NM IN JUNE 2018. DESIGNED TO SPARK A DISCUSSION ABOUT WATER, ECOLOGY, AND THE ACEQUIA SYSTEM, THE COMPLETED ENVIRONMENTALLY-FOCUSED SCULPTURES ARE CURRENTLY INSTALLED IN FRONT OF THE ARTS BUILDING AT NORTHERN NEW MEXICO COLLEGE IN ESPANOLA, NM. TEEN INTERNS PARTICIPATED MORE REGULARLY THAN EVER, ATTENDING PROGRAM BETWEEN 2-5 TIMES PER WEEK THROUGH THE SUMMER MONTHS. INTERNS WORKED HARD TO PLANT, WEED, TEND, AND HARVEST THE HERITAGE CROPS IN THE NORTHERN YOUTH PROJECT GARDEN. ACEQUIA AGRICULTURE REMAINED AN IMPORTANT PART OF OUR PROGRAM WHERE TEEN PARTICIPANTS AND INTERNS REGULARLY WORKED WITH MENTORS TO IRRIGATE THE GARDEN. THE GARDEN OPEN HOUSE, PLANT SALE AND SEED EXCHANGE, AND HARVEST BRUNCH COLLECTIVELY INVITED COMMUNITY PARTICIPANTS TO CELEBRATE TEEN LEADERSHIP ACCOMPLISHMENTS. ARTS SUMMER PROGRAMS INCLUDED EXTENSIVE OUTREACH TO CHILDREN THROUGH PARTNERSHIP WITH REGIONAL ORGANIZATIONS. NORTHERN YOUTH PROJECT MENTOR ARTISTS AND TEENS WORKED WITH ALBUQUERQUE ACADEMY TO CREATE GOURD ART. A TRADITIONAL MICAEOUS POTTERY WORKSHOP LED BY MENTOR ARTIST RIKKI VIERIA TAUGHT NYP MEMBERS, TEENS, INTERNS AND DEL NORTE BOYS AND GIRLS CLUB PARTICIPANTS ABOUT TRADITIONAL POTTERY. FEEDBACK INCLUDED THAT OUR PROGRAM WAS ONE OF THE MOST ENRICHING ACTIVITIES FOR THEIR SUMMER STUDENTS. FELIPE ORTEGA TAUGHT CHILDREN AND YOUTH HOW TO FIRE THE MICACEOUS POTTERY, HELPING CHILDREN AND YOUTH LEARN ABOUT HERITAGE ART TRADITIONS OF NEW MEXICO. NYP MEMBERS ALSO PARTICIPATED IN A T-SHIRT DYING WORKSHOP AT THE ESPANOLA VALLEY FIBER ARTS CENTER. THIS ACTIVITY ENGAGED CHILDREN ENROLLED IN THE NORTHERN YOUTH PROJECT BRIDGE PROGRAM FOR 10-11 YEAR OLDS. TOGETHER WITH REGIONAL ARTISTS, TEENS AND BRIDGE MEMBERS COMPLETED TWO NEW MURALS AT THE NORTHERN YOUTH PROJECT MURAL WALL. AN END OF SUMMER ARTS AND GARDEN FIELD TRIP TO ALBUQUERQUE WRAPPED UP THE SUMMER PROGRAM WITH A PARTNERSHIP WITH LA PLAZITA INSTITUTE. NYP MEMBERS COMPLETED T-SHIRTS WITH THEIR ORIGINAL DESIGN CREATED DURING THE SUMMER PROGRAM (SEE PHOTO). ARTS INTERNS AND CHILDREN PARTICIPANTS FEATURED THEIR WORK AT THE ABIQUIU STUDIO TOUR IN OCTOBER. THE FINALE OF OUR YEAR WAS CELEBRATED AT THE HARVEST BRUNCH WHERE COMMUNITY MEMBERS, FRIENDS, AND FAMILY GATHERED TO CELEBRATE TEEN LEADERSHIP PROJECTS AND THE SEASONAL BOUNTY. TEENS PREPARED AND SERVED THE MEAL, WHICH WAS WELL RECEIVED BY GUESTS. THIS YEAR, STUDENTS WORKED TOGETHER ON TEAM BUILDING PROJECTS, PARTICIPATED IN COOKING CLASSES, COMPLETED A YEAR LONG ARTS PROGRAM, AND MUCH MORE. SUCCESSES SPECIFICALLY INCLUDED THE ONGOING PARTICIPATION OF YOUTH IN OUR PROGRAMS AND THEIR ABILITY TO ACHIEVE NOT JUST AT NORTHERN YOUTH PROJECT BUT IN THEIR LIVES THROUGH GRADUATING FROM HIGH SCHOOL AND ENTERING MEANINGFUL WORK AND/OR COLLEGE.ONE MAJOR SUCCESS OF THE YEAR WAS THE ESTABLISHMENT OF THE SUCCESSFUL "BRIDGE PROGRAM". T.Flexible - create your season of swimmingInclusive - no one sits on a bench on a swim teamTotal - total body workout with little risk of injury Team Structure: The team is divided into the following workout groups. Black, Gold, Silver and Bronze teams and train concurrently, but differing amounts of time in the water, based on age,experience and goals. This gives your swimmer(s) the optimum for both stroke technique and endurance work.The Black team is the fourth level, the elite group of the competitive swim team. This group continues to focus on technique and has qualifying times for Age Group State, Senior State, Sectionals and above.The Gold Team is the third level of the competitive swim team. Continuing to work on technique and working toward qualifying times in JO's Age group/Sr. StateThe Silver team is the second level of the competitive swim team. Focusing on proper stroke technique in coordination with endurance and water-strength work.The Bronze team is our first level of the competitive swim team. Focusing on proper stroke technique in coordination with endurance and water-strength work.Younger swimmers will focus on correct stroke technique, and with age it will remain an emphasis in their training. Practicing a skill incorrectly does not lead to fast swimming and can cause injury. Therefore, we do not move swimmers through the program until the coaches agree on the transition. The coaching staff makes sure your swimmer(s) is ready technically, physically and mentally before moving him/her up to the next level. We do use skill sheets for the Minnows and Intermediate levels and try to test about every four weeks.Our club is a USA Swimming year round competitive swim team offering high quality professional coaching and technique instruction for all ages and abilities. We are the only USA Level 1 Recognized team in Northern Arizona. The goal of our team is to provide every member an opportunity to improve swimming skills and achieve success at his or her level of ability, from novice to international competitor.All of our coaches, as members of USA Swimming, have access to the most comprehensive training and certification program for youth coaches of any sport in the United States. They provide assurances that the time children spend in swimming will be quality time.The Flagstaff Snow Sharks Swim Team, a non profit club, is run by its elected Board of Directors which meets each month. All members are welcome at each meeting and encouraged to be involved in team activities and fundraisers.We are constantly growing and training young swimmers to maintain a well rounded competitive swim team. mission: The New York New Music Ensembles 2017/2018 season explored the transformation of music and experience through shifts in perspective. The first concert of the season on December 18, 2017 at the DiMenna Center for Classical Music featured works by leading European composers spanning three decades. On February 21, 2018, NYNME premiered three new works composed for the ensemble by Brazilian composers Alexandre Lunsqui, Flo Menezes, and Silvio Ferraz. The final of concert of NYNMEs season, on April 9, 2018, explored the augmentation of sonorities through electronic and acoustic perspectives.

name: LITERACY VOLUNTEERS OF SANTA FE
mission: Literacy Volunteers of Santa Fe (LVSF) has served the Santa Fe community for thirty three years, providing literacy instruction for adults and their families. Literacy is essential to improving the quality of life of individuals, promoting economic growth, and building an informed, responsible citizenry in Santa Fe and elsewhere. Since 1985, over 4,714 trained tutors have provided over 487,954 hours of instruction to help more than 13,406 adult students obtain essential skills and reach their fullest potential. This represents volunteer contributions equivalent to over $11 million. We offer programs that provide free, quality tutoring in basic literacy and English as a Second Language, financial literacy, health literacy, citizenship and numeracy skills. Literacy Volunteers of Santa Fe is the only program in Santa Fe County that provides free literacy tutoring services for adults.Literacy Volunteers of Santa Fe has three principal programs: Basic Literacy: Between July 1, 2017 and June 30, 2018, 74 students received 1,780 hours of tutoring in writing and reading. Fifty-five tutors provided these services at multiple sites around Santa Fe County. English as a Second Language: Between July 1, 2017 and June 30, 2018, 305 students received a total of 7,196 hours of tutoring in reading, writing and speaking English. These services were provided by 179 tutors at 13 workplace and community sites. Citizenship Tutoring: Between July 1, 2017 and June 30, 2018, 51 students received 1,033 hours of tutoring to help pass their citizenship exams. Twenty-eight tutors provided these services.Note about funding: In addition to the income specified in this report, Literacy Volunteers (LVSF) of Santa Fe receives funds from state and federal grants that come though the Adult Education Department of Santa Fe Community College. These funds provide salary and administrative support. For the fiscal year ending in June 2018, these funds amounted to almost $80,000.. In addition, the Adult Education Department provides office space and computer and phone support.

name: CHEDER DARCHAI LIMUD
mission: This past year, we continued servicing children in small highly individualized groups of 1-2 children each at either their school location or at a private learning center away from their school. They received support in their religious and secular (reading, writing and math) studies using skill based learning. These children were children who have experienced academic failure and have some kind of learning or behavioral weakness. For children previously at-risk, their gain in academic skill level and taste of school success has greatly impacted their overall self confidence and self esteem. Some of the children that we have serviced for a few continuous years have made much progress and are now fully up to grade level with their peers. Where possible, the curriculum that we have created was used with these children as a support for their class instruction. This was helpful in the children making gains.; In August 2015, the organization began publishing the curriculum and promoting it to schools and parents in the wider community. This included a Hebrew reading curriculum highly graphical, engaging and hands on and textbooks on other Hebrew subjects including Bible and Hebrew language. The Hebrew reading curriculum gives parents and schools the option of remediating reading disabilities using a DIY series of workbooks that have all the professional techniques that specialists use laid out in fun filled exercises with clear instructions. This has proven to be highly effective and spares the parents the need to spend thousands of dollars on remedial programs. The Hebrew Bible curriculum is designed in such a way that the content and architecture of the curriculum allows schools to promote inclusion in their mainstream classroom, as the materials cleverly engage the weakest while simultaneously stimulating and challenging the brightest. As such, in 2017, the decision was made to brand the Hebrew reading books similar to the Bible books as a product to be used in the mainstream classroom promoting inclusion of all children and challenging the gifted students simultaneously. In 2016, a Yiddish edition of the first volume for bilingual students and two more volumes of the English edition were developed. In 2017, another volume of the English edition was created. More volumes are still in the making G-d willing.

name: RON MCBRIDE FOUNDATION INC
mission: IntroductionDuring the first year of operations the Ron McBride Foundation was honored to be supported by a caste of volunteers to carry out its mission. She spent more than 530 hours in her efforts to support the mission of the foundation. These volunteers were not compensated and yet provided nearly $20,000 of their time and talent to the foundation. In summary, the Ron McBride Foundation received the professional and volunteer services of many individuals to commence its first year of operations. The total of their services equals or exceeds $127,950.00 of effort in behalf of the stated mission. It should be noted that Dr. Compton and Mrs. Parson were provided a small stipend of $1,500.00 each for their services.

ATTENDANCE AT THE 2017 OKTOBERFEST EVENT WAS STRONG, BUT EXPENSES EXCEEDED INCOME FOR A SHORTFALL OF APPROXIMATELY $8500. THE HISTORIC ENGINE NO. 1 EXPERIENCED SOME VANDALISM DURING THE YEAR, PUTTING EVEN MORE FOCUS ON CONVINCING THE CITY OF JACKSONVILLE TO APPROVE A STRUCTURE FOR PROTECTION FROM BOTH THE ELEMENTS AND VANDALS. THE BOARD EXPLORED VARIOUS AVENUES FOR FUND RAISING FOR SUCH A STRUCTURE, BUT NOTED THAT MOST SUPPORT IN TOWN WAS BEING DIRECTED AT THE COMMUNITY SENIOR CENTER, WHICH HAD RECEIVED A LARGE MATCHING GRANT.

name: INTERNATIONAL CANCER EXPERT CORPS INC
mission: ICEC MENTORING PARTNERSHIPS/TWINNING PROGRAMSICEC'S MENTORING PARTNERSHIP PROGRAM BRINGS TOGETHER CANCER CARE EXPERTS FROM RESOURCE-RICH SETTINGS WITH HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS IN RESOURCE POOR COUNTRIES TO IMPROVE CANCER PREVENTION, SCREENING, DIAGNOSIS, TREATMENT AND FOLLOW-UP CARE. WITH WELL-DEFINED GOVERNANCE, ESTABLISHED POLICIES AND PROCEDURES, TRANSPARENCY IN OPERATIONS AND THE ABILITY TO LEVERAGE EXPERTISE. ICEC PARTNERS WITH AND ENHANCES ONGOING ACTIVITIES OF GOVERNMENTS, PROF SOCIETIES, CANCER CENTERS AND OTHER NGOS. ICEC ENCOURAGES LOCAL REGIONAL AND NATIONAL INITIATIVES TO DEVELOP SUSTAINABLE CAPACITY AND CAPABILITY IN THE EFFORTS OF THESE COUNTRIES TO BATTLE CANCER. ICEC ESTABLISHED MENTORING PARTNERSHIPS/TWINNING PROGRAMS WITH THE GOALS TO, 1) IMPROVE, FACILITATE AND SUSTAIN POPULATION-DIRECTED CLINICAL CARE AND TRANSLATIONAL CANCER RESEARCH THROUGH PROJECTS CARRIED OUT AT LOCAL CANCER CENTERS BY MULTI-DISCIPLINARY EXPERT TEAMS, 2) TRAIN PHYSICIANS, NURSES, SCIENTISTS, AND OTHER HEALTHCARE & HEALTH POLICY WORKERS IN PUBLIC HEALTH ONCOLOGY AT THESE CENTERS AND 3) ANALYZE LOCAL CANCER CARE SYSTEMS AND MODEL APPROACHES TO STRENGTHEN THEM, 4) ENCOURAGE HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS TO REMAIN IN LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME COUNTRIES (LMIC) RATHER THAN MIGRATE TO UPPER INCOME COUNTRIES FOR EMPLOYMENT, AND 5) CREATE BONA FIDE AND VALUED CAREER PATHS IN ACADEMIA AND PRIVATE PRACTICE FOR HEALTHCARE SERVICE TO THE UNDERSERVED BY PROVIDING AN ORGANIZATIONAL, EDUCATIONAL, RESEARCH AND SERVICE BASE IN ACADEMIC CENTERS OF EXCELLENCE IN RESOURCE-RICH COUNTRIES AND PROFESSIONAL SOCIETIES TO DEVELOP AND SUSTAIN EXPERTS IN PUBLIC HEALTH ONCOLOGY.IN 2017, ICEC DEVELOPED NEW PARTNERSHIPS AND STRENGTHENED ESTABLISHED ONES WITH PROFESSIONAL SOCIETIES AND MAJOR INTERNATIONAL AGENCIES INCLUDING THE AMERICAN SOCIETY OF CLINICAL ONCOLOGY (ASCO), AMERICAN SOCIETY FOR RADIATION ONCOLOGY (ASTRO), ASSOCIATION OF RESIDENTS IN RADIATION ONCOLOGY (ARRO), ROYAL AUSTRALIAN AND NEW ZEALAND COLLEGE OF RADIOLOGISTS (RANZCR), CONSORTIUM OF UNIVERSITIES FOR GLOBAL HEALTH (CUGH), AND THE UNION FOR INTERNATIONAL CANCER CONTROL (UICC). STANDARD OPERATING PROCEDURES FOR MENTORING PARTNERSHIPS WERE CREATED INCLUDING COMPONENTS FOR EXPERTS (MENTORS) IN ICEC HUBS AND ASSOCIATES (MENTEES) IN ICEC CENTERS. THE SET OF METRICS CREATED FOR TRACKING THE PROGRESSION OF ICEC ASSOCIATES AND CENTERS AND USED TO EVALUATE CURRENT CAPABILITIES AND PROVIDE AN UNDERSTANDING OF WHERE INVESTMENT IS NEEDED IS KNOWN AS THE "ICEC 5-STEP PROGRESSION PLAN FOR CANCER CARE" THAT WAS DEVELOPED IN 2016 AND AFTER FURTHER REVIEW WAS INTRODUCED FOR USE IN SELECT TWINNING PROGRAMS. TWINNING PROGRAMS/MENTORING RELATIONSHIPS ARE ALREADY ESTABLISHED IN THE UNITED STATES (NATIVE AMERICANS), CANADA (FIRST NATIONS), GABON, ARMENIA, ALGERIA, TANZANIA, CAMBODIA AND KENYA. ADDITIONAL MENTORING RELATIONSHIPS FOR NEW TWINNING PROGRAMS WERE INITIATED IN COUNTRIES INCLUDING NIGERIA AND KENYA, THE NUMBER OF PEOPLE BENEFITED IS DYNAMIC AS THE REGION'S WORKFORCE CAPABILITY AND CAPACITY INCREASES THROUGH ONGOING MENTORING, TRAINING AND EDUCATION THEREBY IMPROVING THE QUALITY OF CANCER CARE DELIVERED TO ALL PATIENTS PRESENTING WITH CANCER. FOR ADDITIONAL INFORMATION SEE WWW.ICECCANCER.ORG.; EARLY CAREER LEADERS ICEC HAS ESTABLISHED MODELS FOR SUSTAINABLE CAREER PATHS IN ACADEMIA AND IN PRIVATE PRACTICE SO THAT ALTRUISTIC SERVICE CAN BECOME A PILLAR OF HEALTHCARE CAREERS FOR THE EXCEPTION YOUNG HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS SUCH AS THOSE WHO NOW ARE ICEC "EARLY CAREER LEADERS".2017 EARLY CAREER LEADER ACTIVITIES: ICEC ESTABLISHED AN EARLY CAREER LEADERS WORKING GROUP THAT IS COMPRISED OF OUTSTANDING YOUNG PEOPLE IN ONCOLOGY FOCUSING ON CANCER CARE FOR THE UNDERSERVED. THE ICEC EARLY CAREER LEADERS WORKING GROUP OPERATES WITHIN THE ICEC EXPERTS COMMITTEE. ICEC SEEKS FINANCIAL SUPPORT FOR PROGRAMS AND OPERATIONS OF THIS WORKING GROUP WITH THE GOAL OF PROVIDING A REWARDING ACADEMIC CAREER AND LIFE PATH FOR THESE YOUNG MEDICAL PROFESSIONALS TO ADDRESS THE INNUMERABLE CHALLENGING OPPORTUNITIES TO MAKE A SUBSTANTIAL PERSONAL IMPACT ON GLOBAL CANCER CARE.ICEC PROVIDED PEER-REVIEWED GRANTS TO EARLY CAREER LEADERS WHOSE EFFORTS ARE MAKING SIGNIFICANT IMPROVEMENTS IN CANCER CARE IN LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME COUNTRIES (LMICS). BY PROVIDING MENTORING AND FINANCIAL SUPPORT TO THESE DOCTORS, NURSES, PHYSICISTS AND OTHER ALLIED HEALTHCARE PROVIDERS, THEY ARE ABLE TO IMPROVE CANCER CARE IN THESE UNDERSERVED REGIONS WHILE ALSO BUILDING A CAREER THAT BRIDGES THE DIVIDE BETWEEN ACADEMIA AND GLOBAL HEALTH. ONGOING PROGRAMS INCLUDE: 1) GABARONE, BOTSWANA: DEVELOPMENT OF A CANCER CENTER IN PRINCESS MARINA HOSPITAL (UPENN-BOTSWANA PARTNERSHIP), 2) YEREVAN, ARMENIA: IMPROVEMENTS TO THE DELIVERY CARE BY WAY PEDIATRIC ONCOLOGY CARE AND RESEARCH CAPACITY, DEVELOPED A CANCER REGISTRY AND INCREASED TRAINING CAPACITY IN PEDIATRIC HEMATOLOGY, ONCOLOGY AND SURGERY, BUGUNDO MEDICAL CENTER (DUKE), 6) PHOM PENH, SYMPOSIUM DEDICATED TO INCREASE AWARENESS OF CANCER CARE THROUGH AN EXCHANGE OF IDEAS TO IMPROVE CANCER CARE.THE NUMBER OF PEOPLE BENEFITED IS DYNAMIC AS THE INDIVIDUAL EARLY CAREER LEADERS FOCUS ON DIFFERENT CANCERS AND TREATMENT METHODS. EACH UNIQUE PROGRAM ADDRESSES THE DIFFERENT REQUIREMENTS AND CURRENT STATUS OF EXISTING IN-COUNTRY CANCER PROGRAMS. THROUGH MENTORING, EDUCATION AND TRAINING CURRICULUMS, AND BUILDING INDIVIDUAL AND INSTITUITIONAL RELATIONSHIPS, EARLY CAREER LEADERS WORK TO IMPROVE THE SKILLS AND KNOWLEDGE OF THE HEALTHCARE PROVIDERS WITH WHOM THEY WORK, THUS INCREASING THE CAPABILITY AND CAPACITY OF THE HEALTH CARE SYSTEM AND ITS CANCER CARE PROFESSIONALS THEREBY IMPROVING THE QUALITY OF CANCER CARE DELIVERED TO THE LOCAL POPULATIONS.; DEVELOPING NOVEL MEDICAL LINACS FOR CHALLENGING ENVIRONMENTS SUCH AS IN MANY LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME COUNTRIES (LMIC) ICEC'S EFFORTS TO ADDRESS THE CURRENT GAP OF APPROXIMATELY 5,000-10,000 RADIATION TREATMENT MACHINES, PRIMARILY IN LMICS, AS REPORTED BY THE UICC GLOBAL TASK FORCE FOR RADIATION THERAPY FOR CANCER CONTROL AS WELL AS THE GLOBAL NEED TO REDUCE THE THREAT OF RADIOLOGICAL TERRORISM INHERENT IN THE WIDE DISTRIBUTION OF COBALT-60 TREATMENT UNITS, ALSO PRIMARILY IN LMICS, REPRESENT A CONVERGENCE OF THE GOALS AND OBJECTIVES OF NATIONAL AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS. THE SECOND OF TWO INTERNATIONAL WORKSHOPS HOSTED BY THE EUROPEAN ORGANIZATION FOR NUCLEAR RESEARCH (CERN) AND SPONSORED BY ICEC AND THE UK SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY FACILITIES COUNCIL (STFC) WAS HELD ON OCTOBER 26-27, 2017. THIS WORKSHOP, ENTITLED "INNOVATIVE, ROBUST AND AFFORDABLE MEDICAL LINEAR ACCELERATORS FOR CHALLENGING ENVIRONMENTS",BROUGHT TOGETHER LEADING EXPERTS FROM WORLD RENOWNED AGENCIES AND ORGANIZATIONS INCLUDING ENGINEERS, PHYSICISTS, ACADEMICIANS, SCIENTISTS, ECONOMISTS, TECH AND BIO-TECH REPRESENTATIVES, GOVERNMENTAL AND NON-GOVERNMENTAL ORGANIZATIONS SUCH AS US DEPARTMENT OF ENERGY'S NATIONAL NUCLEAR SECURITY AGENCY AND THE INTERNATIONAL ATOMIC ENERGY AGENCY. THE PRIMARY GOAL OF THE WORKSHOP WAS TO IDENTIFY THE PRELIMINARY DESIGN CHARACTERISTICS OF A NOVEL, PROBABLY MODULAR, LINEAR ACCELERATOR TO FILL THE GAP IN NEED FOR RADIATION TREATMENT MACHINES IN CHALLENGING ENVIRONMENTS, PRIMARILY IN LMICS. A SECONDARY GOAL WAS TO REPLACE COBALT-60 MACHINES IN THOSE COUNTRIES WITH NOVEL LINEAR ACCELERATOR TECHNOLOGIES TO REDUCE THE RISK OF NEFARIOUS USE OF UN- OR POORLY-SECURED RADIOACTIVE MATERIALS.FOLLOWING THE OCTOBER 2017 WORKSHOP, FIVE WORK PACKAGES WERE FUNDED BY STFC TO SUPPORT THE FOLLOWING RESEARCH:1. RF POWER SYSTEMS AND OPTIMIZED RF STRUCTURES FOR ELECTRON BEAM ACCELERATION2. ROBUST PERMANENT MAGNET BEAM DELIVERY SYSTEMS FOR MEDICAL RADIOTHERAPY LINACS3. ACCELERATOR TECHNOLOGY OPTIONS STUDY4. LINEAR ACCELERATOR SIMULATIONS FOR STABLE AND SUSTAINABLE OPERATION OF DEVELOPING COUNTRY RADIOTHERAPY LINEAR ACCELERATORS. 5. CLOUD BASED ELECTRONIC INFRASTRUCTURE IN SUPPORT OF LINAC-BASED RADIOTHERAPY IN CHALLENGING ENVIRONMENTSACTIONS FROM THE 2017 WORKSHOP WERE REVIEWED IN A WORKSHOP SPONSORED BY CERN, ICEC AND STFC AND HOSTED BY STFC IN STRETTON, UK, ON MARCH 22-23, 2018, ENTITLED "RE-ENGINEERING FOR THE NEXT GENERATION OF MEDICAL LINEAR ACCELERATORS FOR USE IN CHALLENGING ENVIRONMENTS". A FULL REPORT IS AVAILABLE FOR INTERESTED PARTNERS WITH THE GENERAL CONCLUSIONS THAT THERE ARE NOW OPPORTUNITIES, IDEAS AND INTEREST TO SUPPORT AND PURSUE SUCH AN EFFORT. MORE INFORMATION CAN BE FOUND AT WWW.ICECCANCER.ORG. AT THIS TIME, ICEC IS NOT ABLE TO DETERMINE THE NUMBER OF PEOPLE DIRECTLY BENEFITED BY THE PROGRAM, HOWEVER, THE ANTICIPATED BENEFIT, ONCE THE MACHINE IS DEVELOPED, WILL BE HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF PEOPLE IN LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME COUNTRIES AND IN CHALLENGING ENVIRONMENTS WHO WILL HAVE ACCESS TO EFFECTIVE AND SAFE CANCER TREATMENT AND MUCH NEEDED PALLIATIVE CARE FOR THOSE WITH ADVANCED DISEASE.

name: SAN BRUNO MOUNTAIN WATCH
mission: Stewardship :Our Stewardship Programs involve local communities in ecological restoration projects, thereby providing opportunities where people improve the health of San Bruno Mountain's habitats while they connect with and learn about the mountain. Our stewardship efforts take place on various parts of San Bruno Mountain and occur every week throughout the year. The programs include the "Stewardship Mountaineers", "Dune Defenders", "South San Francisco Weed Warriors" and "Guadalupe Valley Stewards". Volunteer participants in these programs include local schools, corporate groups and businesses, residents, youth groups and community groups. In 2017 we facilitated 2820 hours of volunteer restoration work that included native plant revegetation and invasive plant removal.O; Mission Blue Nursery Program:The Mission Blue Nursery is a native plant nursery at the base of San Bruno Mountain in Brisbane, California that specializes in growing native plants sourced exclusively by permit from seeds and cuttings on San Bruno Mountain. The plants grown at the nursery were provided for a variety of habitat restoration programs on San Bruno Mountain, for the benefit of grassland habitat for the endangered Mission Blue and Callippe Silversopot butterflies and for the restoration of Colma Creek. Plants from the nursery also enhanced urban and suburban landscapes, as they were utilized in school gardens, sidewalk gardens and home gardens in various parts of the San Francisco Bay Area. Volunteers contributed 1775 hours of nursery work including potting up plants, tending our demonstration garden and maintaining plant health. In the Fall of 2017 efforts successfully began to re-organize and expand the nursery production and table areas in order to double the capacity of our nursery to produce and store plants.; Education: Our Education Program provided environmental education opportunities to a variety of students in the vicinity of San Bruno Mountain on a variety of relevant themes. We launched an education program focused on the San Bruno Mountain Dunes, engaging schools on the western side of San Bruno Mountain with classroom presentations, guided field trips and service-learning restoration events. Schools participating in this program included Susan B. Anthony Elementary, Skyline College, the Hilldale School and Westborough Middle School. We also collaborated with Lipman Middle School to create educational opportunities for students that involved exploring different themes related to native plants while students practiced the scientific method. For example we guided students in the implementation of experiments that tested the effects of various types of soil textures on the growrh of different San Bruno Mountain native plant species. Field trips and restoration events on the mountain were provided as well to other schools including Compass High School, Panorama Elementary School, Green Hills Elementary School and Hillsborough High School. We also provided presentations at other schools and places of learning including Notre Dame de Namur University, San Francisco State University and the San Francisco Public Library. Furthermore, San Bruno Mountain Watch Board Members provided nearly 40 free guided hikes to the public on the mountain, helping raise awareness about the unique natural and cultural history of the mountain.; Advocacy and Land Conservation:San Bruno Mountain Watch Board Members and staff encouraged local government officials and members of the public to support conservation and land acquistion efforts on San Bruno Mountain in order to protect parcels of land on the mountain that are not protected as public open space, including portions of the San Bruno Mountain dunes and the northern side of Sign Hill.

name: VIABLE OPTIONS INC
mission: IN 2017, THE VISION FOR VIABLE OPTIONS UNDERWENT A DRAMATIC SHIFT. AS WE ENGAGED IN THE WORLD OF PREGNANCY CARE, WE WERE CONFRONTED WITH A POLARIZED POLITICAL WORLD FUELED BY AGENDA AND IDEOLOGY, IN WHICH HOLISTIC CARE WAS ALMOST ALWAYS ABSENT FROM THE SERVICES AND APPROACH OFFERED BY AGENCIES, ORGANIZATIONS, INSTITUTIONS, AND INDIVIDUALS. FOR THE PAST 40 YEARS, THE NATIONAL CONVERSATION SURROUNDING UNINTENDED PREGNANCY HAS BEEN PRIMARILY APPROACHED THROUGH THE LENS OF POLITICS. NO LONGER IS PREGNANCY VIEWED AS A PERSONAL AFFAIR TO BE ADDRESSED BY INDIVIDUALS, FAMILIES, AND COMMUNITIES. TODAY, IT IS A DIVISIVE SOCIAL ISSUE. THE FOCUS OF CARE AND CONCERN HAS GREATLY SHIFTED AWAY FROM THE NEEDS OF PREGNANT WOMEN AND ONTO THE PROTECTION OF AN AGENDA AND THE PURSUIT OF AN IDEOLOGICAL VICTORY. ALL TOO OFTEN INFORMATION REGARDING THE DECISIONAL OUTCOMES OF UNINTENDED PREGNANCY IS POLITICIZED AND FREQUENTLY SHARED THROUGH CAREFUL SELECTION AND OMISSION WHICH REFLECTS PERSONAL OR ORGANIZATIONAL BIAS. EDUCATION SHOULD NEVER BE POLITICIZED AND INFORMATION SHOULD NEVER BE WITHHELD. SHARING SELECTIVE, PARTIAL, OR INACCURATE INFORMATION IN ORDER TO PROTECT A PERSONAL BELIEF OR IDEOLOGY IS A FORM OF MANIPULATION - A GRIEVOUS INJUSTICE TO ALL THOSE SEEKING GUIDANCE AND SUPPORT. VIABLE OPTIONS IS BREAKING THE BARRIERS OF THE BINARY WORLD OF "PRO" VS. "ANTI" TO PROVIDE THE THIRD CHOICE - AN APPROACH TO UNINTENDED PREGNANCY THAT IS NON-POLITICAL, NON-MANIPULATIVE, AND RELATIONAL. WE ARE CONFRONTING CULTURAL PATTERNS INTEGRATED DEEP INTO OUR SOCIETAL BEHAVIOR AND MINDSET. THIS TYPE OF CULTURAL CHANGE IS A LONG-TERM PROCESS, BUT ONE WE FULLY EXPECT TO SEE. IT REQUIRES ACTIVE ENGAGEMENT IN OUR COUNTY, REGION, AND BEYOND - EQUIPPING INDIVIDUALS, FAMILIES, AND COMMUNITIES TO RESPOND HOLISTICALLY TO THE ISSUES OF UNINTENDED PREGNANCY IN THEIR OWN SPHERES. IT REQUIRES TEACHING PEOPLE TO LEAD WITH RELATIONSHIP, CARE, AND CONCERN-NOT PERSONAL OPINION-AND TO BECOME THE SOLUTION TO THE PRACTICAL NEEDS OF THOSE FACING AN UNINTENDED PREGNANCY. IN A WORLD IN WHICH WE HAVE BEEN CONDITIONED TO RESPOND POLITICALLY AND IDEOLOGICALLY TO THE ISSUES OF UNINTENDED PREGNANCY, A RELATIONAL RESPONSE IS UNCOMFORTABLE AND COUNTER INTUITIVE. AND IN ORDER TO MOBILIZE OUR CULTURE IN THE THIRD CHOICE APPROACH, WE MUST FIRST PROVIDE A NEW "LENS" WHICH RESTORES A FOCUS ON RELATIONSHIP AND MEETING THE NEEDS OF THE INDIVIDUAL. NO LONGER CAN WE SIMPLY VOTE OUR CONSCIENCE OR GIVE MONEY TO THE NONPROFIT OF OUR CHOICE. WE MUST NOW SEEK TO BECOME, IN SOME WAY, THE ANSWERS TO THE NEEDS OF WOMEN, MEN, AND FAMILIES FACING UNINTENDED PREGNANCIES. IF WE DESIRE TO EMPOWER WOMEN WHO FACE THESE DECISIONS, TO CARE FOR THEM, AND TO SEE THEM PROSPER, IT IS NECESSARY TO RECOGNIZE THAT POLITICS IS NOT THE ANSWER. OUR APPROACH IS RADICAL. IT DOESN'T FIT INTO THE CURRENT CULTURAL LANDSCAPE. BUT OUR GOAL IS FOR THE THIRD CHOICE TO BECOME COMMONPLACE AND FOR UNINTENDED PREGNANCY TO SHIFT FROM A BINARY FRAME OF "PRO" VS. "ANTI" TO ONE OF RELATIONAL ADVOCACY AND SUPPORT - RECOGNIZING WOMEN'S STORIES DON'T END WITH A PREGNANCY DECISION AND THAT THE GREATEST NEED OF EACH PERSON IS RELATIONSHIP. PREGNANCY MUST BE RECLAIMED FROM THE POLITICAL STAGE AND THE RESPONSIBILITY FOR WOMEN'S CARE RETURNED TO COMMUNITIES, FAMILIES, AND PROFESSIONAL, NONPOLITICAL AGENCIES. THIS REQUIRES INVESTMENT IN THE NEXT GENERATION, CHANGING THE NARRATIVE IN OUR INDIVIDUAL COMMUNITIES, AND PLANTING SEEDS OF COMPASSION AND HOPE THAT WILL TAKE ROOT IN THE HEARTS OF THOSE WHO WILL ONE DAY STAND IN OUR PLACE. NO LONGER DOES PREGNANCY NEED TO BE POLITICIZED. NO LONGER DOES EDUCATION AND INFORMATION NEED TO BE AGENDA DRIVEN. NO LONGER DOES POLITICS HAVE TO INFLUENCE PERSONAL CHOICE. HOPE FOR THOSE FACING PREGNANCY DECISIONS LIES IN THE WILLINGNESS OF COMMUNITY MEMBERS TO LAY ASIDE THEIR POLITICAL VIEWS AND WORK TOGETHER TO SERVE AND SUPPORT THEM. AND ALTHOUGH IT MAY SEEM IMPOSSIBLE TO CHANGE THE CULTURE SURROUNDING THE CONVERSATION OF PREGNANCY, WHAT IS RIGHT CAN NEVER TRULY BE IMPOSSIBLE. IN 2017, VIABLE OPTIONS' VISION EXPANDED TO INCLUDE ACTIVE ENGAGEMENT WITH THE COMMUNITY THROUGH MARKETING, EDUCATION, PRESENTATIONS, MEETINGS, DESIGNS, AND TABLING, IN ORDER TO BRING THE THIRD CHOICE TO OUR COUNTY. THIS BECAME A CENTRAL PRIORITY AND FOCUS OF OUR ORGANIZATION IN 2017, HELPING TO REFINE OUR STRATEGIES AND GOALS. COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT IN 2017, VIABLE OPTIONS MADE COMMUNITY ENGAGEMENT A CENTRAL PRIORITY - LOOKING TO EDUCATE THOSE IN OUR COUNTY ON THE THIRD CHOICE APPROACH AND EQUIPPING PEOPLE TO RESPOND TO THE ISSUES OF UNINTENDED PREGNANCY IN A NON-POLITICAL, NON-MANIPULATIVE, AND RELATIONAL WAY. THIS REQUIRED MANY MEETINGS WITH INDIVIDUALS FROM THE EDUCATIONAL, SOCIAL SERVICE, GOVERNMENTAL, MEDICAL, AND RELIGIOUS COMMUNITIES. THROUGHOUT THE YEAR, WE CONDUCTED OVER 120 MEETINGS - NOT ONLY INTRODUCING LOCAL ORGANIZATIONS AND PROFESSIONALS TO THE WORK AND SERVICES OF VIABLE OPTIONS, BUT MORE IMPORTANTLY, HELPING THEM TO UNDERSTAND THE THIRD CHOICE APPROACH. 30 OF THESE MEETINGS INCLUDED TOURS OF VIABLE OPTIONS WHERE PEOPLE WERE ABLE TO SEE FIRST HAND, OUR LOCATION AND HOW WE SERVE THOSE COMING THROUGH OUR DOORS. THESE MEETINGS ALLOWED US TO FURTHER OUR MISSION THROUGHOUT THE COUNTY AS WE WERE GIVEN OPPORTUNITY TO SHARE WITH INDIVIDUALS, SPEAK AT COALITIONS, AND PRESENT AT COMMUNITY CLUBS. THE THIRD CHOICE PUBLICATION STARTING IN MAY OF 2017, A PRIMARY PROJECT WAS THE DESIGN AND RELEASE OF OUR PUBLICATION, THE THIRD CHOICE - A BOOKLET DESIGNED TO COMMUNICATE TO OUR COMMUNITY AND CULTURE OUR UNIQUE APPROACH TO THE ISSUE OF UNINTENDED PREGNANCY. THE PROJECT, IN ITS ENTIRETY, ACCOUNTED FOR ROUGHLY 400 STAFF HOURS. INCLUDING 24 PAGES OF METICULOUSLY FORMULATED IDEAS, THIS PUBLICATION BREAKS DOWN THE PROBLEM CURRENTLY FACING OUR CULTURE REGARDING UNINTENDED PREGNANCY, OUR SOLUTION TO THAT PROBLEM, OUR VISION FOR THE FUTURE, AND THE PRACTICAL STEPS FOR BECOMING INVOLVED WITH VIABLE OPTIONS. IT INTRODUCES THE THIRD CHOICE-AN APPROACH TO UNINTENDED PREGNANCY THAT IS NON-POLITICAL, NON-MANIPULATIVE, AND RELATIONAL. IT IS AN APPROACH THAT FOCUSES ON MEETING THE NEEDS OF THE INDIVIDUAL IN ORDER TO EMPOWER THEM TO MAKE A CHOICE THAT IS WHOLLY THEIRS - LOOKING TO COMMUNITIES, INDIVIDUALS, AND FAMILIES AS THE SOLUTION FOR THE NEEDS OF THOSE FACING A PREGNANCY DECISION. 2500 COPIES WERE PRINTED AND HUNDREDS WERE DISTRIBUTED THROUGHOUT THE REMAINDER OF THE YEAR TO MEMBERS OF THE COMMUNITY, PROFESSIONAL AGENCIES, AND THE LOCAL EDUCATIONAL INSTITUTIONS. GALA IN OCTOBER OF 2017, WE HELD OUR ANNUAL GALA. THIS EVENT IS A STAPLE IN OUR CALENDAR EACH YEAR, AS IT SERVES AS AN OPPORTUNITY TO FRAME FOR OUR DONOR COMMUNITY OUR MISSION AND APPROACH TO UNINTENDED PREGNANCY. WITH WELL OVER 130 PEOPLE IN ATTENDANCE, THE NIGHT WAS NOT ONLY AN OPPORTUNITY TO RAISE FUNDS SPECIFICALLY FOR THE OPERATIONS OF VIABLE OPTIONS, BUT TO SHARE WITH OUR DONOR COMMUNITY OUR EXPANDING VISION, WHICH INCLUDED ADDING A NEW STAFF MEMBER TO OUR TEAM. VIABLE OPTIONS' APPROACH AS A NONPOLITICAL INTERMEDIARY IN THE CULTURAL CONVERSATION OF UNINTENDED PREGNANCY IS NONTRADITIONAL AND REQUIRES A GREAT DEAL OF EXPLANATION, EDUCATION, AND FRAMING. AT EACH YEAR'S GALA, WE UPDATE OUR DONORS ON OUR ACTIVITIES AND GROWTH AND DISCUSS THE OUTWORKING AND IMPORTANCE OF THE THIRD CHOICE - BEING NON-POLITICAL, NON-MANIPULATIVE, AND RELATIONAL.

name: UNITED PAWS OF TILLAMOOK
mission: ClinicUPs original focus was spay/neuter (S/N) and continues as our key to success. With the momentum and heritage of 1,000 s/ns per year, UP sees the feasibility of stabilizing the countys cat population. Focused s/n success of 70-90% by target areas (like towns) have been documented to stabilize populations. The key is to focus on limited geographical targets one at a time. This will require us to increase s/ns to 1,400-2,000/yr for 5-6 years until we expect the cat population to stabilize reducing s/ns to700/year. Our target areas will gradually move around the entire county. A side benefit will be a greatly reduced annual death of outdoor kittens and cats. Kitten deaths are very high in the first year. Continuously pregnant cats die young. High Impact targeted s/n can mitigate both items.; FOSTER ADOPTION PROGRAM. UPT provides the life saving service of re-homing relinquished and rescued companion animals. These cats, and some dogs, are placed in caring, experienced foster homes until, through our promotions utilizing monthly Adoptathons, local advertising, online pet placement databases, and UPTs Facebook page, a loving new forever home is found. In 2013 UPT placed about 250 pets in new homes.; Medical Support: Through partnerships with local aid organizations and requests for help left on our Hotline, United Paws helps subsidize the most needy pet guardians and community cat colony caregivers with high quality pet food they would otherwise be unable to provide, and provide needed medical services for pets from low-income households.; Rescue & Trapping. Emergency services are provided to quickly locate and save an animal in danger of abandonment or of a threat. Trapping of at risk animals in the community. We are now able to provide shelter in the building acquired in 2016. We provide temporary housing for animals that have been abandoned, rescued or relinquished at the request of local service organizations, such as Law enforcement and hospice. Once foster homes become available, cats and kittens are transferred while awaiting adoption.

name: TORRINGTON POLICE ACTIVITIES LEAGUE INC
mission: After School ProgramsOur Afterschool Programs grew to consistent daily offerings in four schools four days aweek, providing parents and teachers with a valuable resource. We found marked differences in kids as a result of operating the After school Program, PAL Scholars, in these schools. Please visit our website for testimonials and for success stories at www.torringtonpal.org. Due to the large visibility of our growing after school presence, our other programs also grew and began to work in tandem for the betterment of our members. In fact we found that by growing our after school program we know were able to touch kids more consistently and frequently with better results. For example, if a student was enrolled in after school, we encouraged them to also enroll in our rec programs. With practices, games and afterschool, we began mentoring kids with the volunteer help of police and community leaders 3-5 times a week. We worked closely with teachers to follow up on kids going through tough behavior or family issues to encourage them to do well in the classroom through their participation with PAL. They simply didn't want to miss out on learning or the fun to be had in after school which helped educators and parents give these kids goals to shoot for at home or in the classroom.; Summer CampWe also significantly increased our program offerings in the summer by partnering to offer a new end of summer camp experience for kids designated at risk or on the brink to help prepare them for school and to start the school year off well. This dynamic summer programming kept the kids engaged and focused for the school year ahead. Many were very successful in transitioning the learning from the summer to he school year. We also saw increased enrollments in our programs as a result of their connections to PAL from the summer. Our College Bound/Education First programming--which brings low income and diverse ethnic, "first generation" kids to area colleges for tours and programming, also saw an expansion of services and trips. We actively began partnering our services to other town highschools in our region to offer these trips with great success.

name: PASSION 4 PEOPLE INTERNATIONAL INC
mission: TOGETHER IN 2017: GIVING HIM THE HONOR WITH YOU! We shared the Good News face-to-face with at least 6913 people. Helped 775 people respond to Gods offer of salvation & restoration. Helped over 665 receive training in discipleship & Friendship Evangelism. Our team prayed for and washed the feet of children and gave over 1365 pairs of flip-flops & sandals in the slums of India. 537 believers trained in our Foundations Course and Celebrate Recovery in India, Nepal and here in the USA. The year 2017 was a year of going deeper and further. Deeper work in our local churches as we worked to mentor 5 evangelists, David, Israel, Austin, Chris, and Jon. It was a deeper work in India as our evangelists spent three weeks studying the Gospel message and how to follow up with those from other religious backgrounds. It was a year of going further with 10 new Celebrate Recovery groups starting in Hyderabad. It was a year of going further as we took 15 believers from Oregon and Washington to India last month. Our team ministered to over 5,135 people in 33 gatherings. There were 721 recorded decisions to follow Jesus! MASTER TRAINERS IMPACT- Our 6 master trainers in India have trained 255 other evangelists these past 6 months in the use of the Foundations Discipleship Class and these have taught over 600 people. Together, three of our master trainers have reached over 6,600 people with the Gospel with at least 335 baptisms. Austin Hall (P4PI Team Evangelist) - Ever since coming back from Romania last fall, Austin couldnt ignore the burden to do evangelism in Portland as he had done in Romania. We began to pray for open doors and the Lord provided! In 2017, Austin has spoken four times at various schools and one youth group. There have been 66 decisions for Christ among the 250 plus high school and college students he has spoken to. Francis, Sandra, Daniel & Shiloh Bezzam are missionaries to South Asians in Portland. Francis and his family have settled in Portland to join us in reaching South Asians. They have already begun making a real difference as they are co-leading our Indian Campus, meeting many immigrants and inviting them into relationship. Francis is working to host a fundraiser for an Indian-run nonprofit in February which will most likely draw as many as 500 South Asians. Mary Davis & Judy Armstrong mobilized 60 women at Grace Point Community to make bookmarks and memory verse purses with Scripture for over 500 women in India. The OR/WA team gave them away during their trip in November. Criss Firebaugh lead many to Christ in the villages and has started a project to equip her Indian church-planting partners to show the Jesus Film. This past year P4PI equipped our 6 evangelist groups with projectors. Criss is helping take that to the next level and to evangelists who are going to even more remote places. Jen, and I co-lead a team to Cuba as part of our work to train evangelists and believers at our church, Sonrise. We saw 52 people give their lives to Christ. Our evangelists at Sonrise, David and Israel, both came away with new tools to train Gods people and a plan to continue doing so at home and again in Cuba. Weve been doing regular evangelism and disciple-making training with our Indian Campus small group, our India & Cuba mission teams and local evangelists. Weve also been working with other Christian neighbors to reach our neighborhood. In fact, our neighborhood Easter egg hunt at a local elementary school drew over 500 people. The What Is Easter? booth had a steady stream of people receiving gospel tracts and a presentation by youth using the Evangacube. We also distributed 115 Christmas gift bags of cookies and invited neighbors to come to Christmas Services. WHATS AHEAD IN 2018: The Luis Palau Association has invited me to join a team of leaders to help increase evangelism in the local church. Well be working together to bring a training conference in May to Portland. Im also teaching a track on Hinduism at Mission Connexion Conference this coming January 19-20. Scott Miller joined me in Hyderabad to introduce and train a new group of pastors to run CR. The response was tremendous. Well be launching 6 new groups in three new states of India starting in January! Ive finished my Doctorate class work! In 2018, Ill be making may main focus my doctoral project to develop tools for helping pastors identify, equip, and mobilize evangelists within their churches. I believe re-positioning the evangelist in the local church is vital in our time. Indian Team to Uganda- Dr. Tim Robnett is leading a unique campaign of evangelism for our Multnomah students and Indian Outreach Specialists in Kampala in May 2018.
