name: AMY D FOUNDATION
mission: Amy D. Summer Sessions The Amy D. Summer Sessions is a program that provides mentoring on bikes for young girls ages 7-14. The program furthers the Organization's purpose by increasing participation in the sport of cycling and by using the sport of cycling to teach girls fundamental skills related to personal development, healthy competition and goal setting. The Amy D. Summer Sessions program also aims to create a community that empowers girls through sport and helps girls recognize the positive effects of strong female bonds. The program is a collaboration with, and conducted by, the Little Bellas, another non-profit organization with nine years of programming experience. The Amy D. Summer Sessions consist of eight different sessions throughout the course of the summer, which are held at regional parks that feature well-maintained trail networks with a diverse level of difficulty. The Organization has held at least one Amy D. Summer Session (consisting of eight individual sessions) since its formation in January 2014. During a typical Summer Session, the program participants are joined with female mentors in programs that use mountain biking as a vehicle to teach the importance of teamwork, goal-setting and a healthy lifestyle. Mentors and girls ride together at local trail networks, focusing on improving technical skills as well as participating in team-building activities. The Amy D. Summer Sessions are organized around a curriculum that builds upon previous skills, and girls are broken up into groups based on age and ability. After the group ride, the groups participate in games that incorporate that particular day's skill focus. Each session also includes the ever important snack. Mentoring on the trail is conducted by developing a level of trust with the participants and implementing planned curriculum that focuses on skills progression and building confidence. Experience within the Little Bellas program has shown that girls bring life challenges with them and work through these challenges organically while riding with their peers and mentors. While there is no planned curriculum for the Summer Sessions that addresses body image, positive self-talk, bullying, fear or anxiety, mentors are coached on how to work through these issues if they arise among program participants, thereby providing the participants with mentorship that extends beyond cycling and to matters the program participants may face on a daily basis. The Amy D. Summer Sessions' mentors consist of a diverse volunteer group of active women cyclers who identify with the Little Bellas' and the Organization's mission and are passionate about riding bicycles. The mentors are typically solicited by the Organization from a pool of volunteers that the Organization has previously worked with or been introduced to, but are generally considered to be affiliated with both the Organization and the Little Bellas during the Amy D. Summer Sessions. Consistency is very important to building a successful bond with the girls in the program; therefore, the quality of the program depends a great deal on the commitment from mentors. As a result of this, each mentor is expected to attend at least 75% of scheduled program days. In addition to regular mentors, vetted professional female cyclists are invited to meet and mentor every girl in the program. As a result of the Organization's desire to provide each participant with a quality experience, the number of participants in each Summer Session is limited to approximately 30 girls due to the capacity of the facilities and the number of experienced mentors available to participate in each Summer Session. The program is open to all girls ages 7-14, and there is a $200 fee for participation in the program, which includes participation in all eight session dates and a custom designed cycling jersey. The $200 participation fee is collected by the Little Bellas. However, the Little Bellas also offers an unlimited number of scholarships pursuant to which the $200 fee is waived or reduced, which are available upon request. The fees collected from participants in the Summer Sessions help offset a portion of the costs of operating the program. Based on the experience of the Little Bellas administration, the Organization believes that associating a monetary value with the program helps foster a dedication to the program and establishes commitment from program participants, which is essential for successful execution of the Summer Sessions. Applications for the Amy D. Summer Sessions are available online through the Little Bellas' or the Organization's website. Announcement and outreach regarding the open application period (which occurs annually, beginning in early February) is performed through the Little Bellas' and the Organization's social media, web and email outlets. The relationship between Little Bellas and the Organization is such that the production of the Amy D. Summer Sessions is made possible through the sharing of responsibilities. The Organization provides management oversight for the Amy D. Summer Sessions and contributes financial resources by sharing the costs of the Amy D. Summer Sessions with the Little Bellas. The Little Bellas is also responsible for management and oversight of the Amy D. Summer Sessions, including accepting applications from participants and mentors, planning activities and on-site execution. The Organization is responsible for site-specific costs and certain management-related matters, which include, among other things, (1) facility usage fees, (2) purchase, storage and provision of equipment and supplies, (3) food and snacks, and (4) communication and planning of activities with the community and officials. Other costs associated with management and oversight of the Amy D. Summer Sessions are paid for by the Little Bellas. The sharing of responsibilities and financial resources between the two organizations allows the Amy D. Summer Sessions to enroll a greater number of participants than otherwise would be possible. Without the financial and human resources support of the Organization and the Little Bellas, the Amy D. Summer Sessions would not be possible. The Organization's expenses for each Summer Session (consisting of eight individual sessions) are typically about $3,000. The largest single expense is site usage fees, which typically cost the Organization between $1,000-$1,500. In addition to the expenses listed above, the Organization also incurs expenses related to the promotion of the programming through web and social media outlets, and the occasional hosting of gathering events for staff members.; Amy D. Road Cycling Amy D. Road Cycling is a developmental racing program sponsored by the Organization that increases opportunities for talented and driven women to compete at the elite level of road cycling in a supportive and structured environment. The program focuses on team cycling events and pairing up-and-coming athletes with seasoned veterans. Through the oversight of experienced members of the Organization and on-the-ground support from a professional staff, the members of the Amy D. Road Cycling team are united by common goals that facilitate growth through breakdown of personal limitations. The Amy D. Road Cycling program builds a team of six to eight athletes per event and provides the team with the support of a professional management staff, consisting of a "Directeur Sportif" (team director), a mechanic and a "soigneur" (a member of the team staff that looks after the riders). The staff acts in supervisory, coaching and mentoring roles throughout the course of an event. Active communication before and after each competition is achieved through formal and informal team meetings and practices. The Directeur Sportif manages the program on the ground during the event and is typically a female figure with extensive professional cycling experience who identifies with the mission of the Organization. The mechanic and soigneur (male or female) serve in supporting roles under the Directeur and also have extensive experience in their respective positions. The Organization is responsible for the oversight of the program scope, tasking staff with responsibilities and providing equipment and supplies. Additionally, the Organization covers direct expenses for participation in a particular event (e.g., travel, registration, lodging, food) and covers compensation of the professional management staff and of the Organization's employees who oversee the program. The Amy D. Road Cycling program occurs at locations throughout the United States at established road cycling events governed by the Union Cycliste Internationale ("UCI"). The Amy D. Road Cycling program focuses participation in key events throughout the course of the UCI road cycling season (which runs from approximately April-September). Generally, each event is three to seven consecutive days in duration. The Amy D. Road Cycling program debuted in 2015 with attendance at the Tour of the Gila (located in New Mexico) and USA Pro Challenge (located in Colorado) events. The Organization expects to attend additional events throughout the United States in the future. The Organization does not place age restrictions on the women who may participate in the program. The Amy D. Road Cycling program strives to provide new opportunities for young, developing athletes and established athletes alike by bringing them together in a constructive environment. Women are selected for events within the program through a combination of active scouting and an open application process based on current trajectory determined through analysis of personal results and references within the cycling community. The primary objectives of the Amy D. Road Cycling program are: (1) to build greater opportunities for driven women in the sport of cycling who may not otherwise have the ability to participate due to an inherent lack of support, and (2) to create a constructive cycle of positive personal development by bringing up-and-coming talented athletes together with experienced competitors and managers in order to facilitate direct mentoring and coaching. For example, the UCI mandates that all participants at sanctioned cycling events be members of a registered team, which thereby inherently leads to the exclusion of individual registrants. If a team lacks the financial resources necessary to field a team of riders at a particular event (which commonly occurs at the highest level of women's professional cycling), then the individual riders' only hope of participating in the event is by "guest riding" on another team in attendance. Therefore, the Organization creates opportunities for women in the sport of cycling by organizing teams with open rosters that may vary from event-to-event. Furthermore, given that the Organization covers the direct expenses associated with participation in an event, the Organization creates opportunities for individuals and teams that otherwise would not have the financial resources to participate in a particular event. Total expenses for the Organization with respect to the Amy D. Road Cycling program range from $5,000-$10,000 per event and consist of covering the direct expenses of participants, such as lodging, food, registration, and compensation of the professional management staff, as well as compensation of Organization employees who oversee the program. Typically, some expenses (e.g., lodging) can be eliminated by leveraging resources within the community. Some additional funding may come from corporate sponsorship and donations.; Amy D. Cyclocross Amy D. Cyclocross is a developmental racing program that increases opportunities for talented and driven women to compete at the elite level of the sport of cyclocross in a supportive and structured environment. The program features two components: (1) an open division, and (2) a U-23 (under age 23) division. The open division provides the comprehensive support needed to elevate athletes to the highest level in the sport, carefully selecting women that embody extreme drive, passion and focus. The U-23 division provides complimentary support to interested young women in an environment that promotes a healthy lifestyle balance. Both the open division and the U-23 division of the program feature focused coaching from professional staff and mentoring from veteran athletes to help participants reach their full potential through a season of competition. Experienced members of the Organization oversee the program and professional staff assist with the day-to-day operations of the program. The Amy D. Cyclocross program provides opportunities for young, talented and developing athletes by placing them in a constructive environment where they have the opportunity to learn from professional staff and concerned mentors. Similar to the Amy D. Road Cycling program, the primary objectives of the Amy D. Cyclocross program are: (1) to build greater development opportunities for women in the sport of cyclocross in order to facilitate growth in participation and promote the pursuit of lofty goals, particularly in the face of a demonstrated lack of current support for women within the sport, and (2) to create a constructive cycle of positive personal development by bringing up-and-coming talented athletes together with experienced competitors and managers in order to facilitate direct mentoring and coaching. Objective (2) above is further supported by engaging the participants in mentoring the younger participants and the girls in the Amy D. Summer Sessions, thereby providing examples of progression in action and reinforcing the importance of positive role models and strong female bonds. Potential participants in the Amy D. Cyclocross program are evaluated through an open application process consisting of a written and interview component. The Organization works closely with the Raleigh-Clement Professional Cyclocross Team, one of the foremost cyclocross programs in the country, in order to provide participants with a consistently high quality support structure from which they may benefit. In the future, the Organization expects that growth will likely be met through building partnerships with additional organizations, such as Olympian Mountain Biker Ann Trombley's TrailMaster Coaching and new non-profit Women In Sports Enrichment (WISE). The Amy D. Cyclocross program coincides with the cyclocross competition season, which typically runs from late August to Early January. The schedule is based on local and national cyclocross events governed by the UCI and USA Cycling ("USAC"), along with appropriate planning regarding a particular participant's age, experience and other life commitments. The Amy D. Cyclocross program occurs at locations throughout the United States at established cyclocross events governed by the UCI or USAC. The Organization supported participants in the Amy D. Cyclocross program in the Fall of 2014 and 2015. The Amy D. Cyclocross program features an open application process, announced through web and social media channels in the Spring of the applicable year. The application consists of a set of written questions regarding the applicant's experience and goals, as well as a set of open-ended questions regarding her perspective on the mission of the Organization and her involvement in the execution of that mission. A narrow subset of applicants are selected for a phone interview with the program oversight committee (which consists of members of the Organization and the Raleigh-Clement Professional Cyclocross Team), at which point the final selection is made. Total expenses to the Organization with respect to the Amy D. Cyclocross program are approximately $15,000 per rider per season, including travel, lodging, meals and incidentals, equipment and staff support (e.g., bicycle mechanic). The Amy D. Cyclocross program is heavily subsidized with in-kind infrastructure and management support from the Raleigh-Clement Professional Cyclocross Team. Equipment costs are typically small due to support from bicycle industry partners.

name: WATKINS MILL ASSOCIATION INC
mission: Watkins Mill Association proactively supports the preservation and living history of Watkins Woolen Mill State Historic Site. Watkins Mill is the last textile mill in the United States with its original machinery still intact. The Association promoted the Mill to be recognized by the United States Department of Interior as a National Historical Landmark, the National Register of Historic Places, a Clay County Historic Landmark, and a National Mechanical Engineering Landmark. The Association turned the Historic Site into a destination, restoring Watkins' Home, Mill, Chapel, one-room Schoolhouse and farm buildings. It worked. Watkins Mill is now the region's premier historic attraction. During 2017, there were 16,951 Historic Site Visitors and 544,549 Park Visitors. Data shows they come from all over Missouri, as well as many zip codes in Kansas, Illinois, Nebraska, Iowa, Arkansas and beyond. Visiting the Historic Site is like stepping into the 19th Century. Many of the buildings that Waltus Watkins built over half a century - including the family home and three-story woolen mill - are preserved to provide Visitors a sense of life in the 1870s. College professors and K-12 teachers often include Watkins Mill in curricula for its historical importance to entrepreneurs in frontier life, the Industrial Revolution and Civil War. In partnership with Missouri State Parks, the Association has cultivated an 1870s non-traditional community venue which encourages historic, educational, cultural, and recreational programs. 2017 activities included these popular annual events: Volunteer Recognition Dinner, Fall on the Farm, Get Outdoors Day 6K Run, Living History interpretive weekends, and Christmas on the Farm in the Watkins Home. The Association's Harvest Gala, a new annual fundraiser now in its second year, generated a 66% revenue increase over year one.

name: REACHING OUT FROM WITHIN
mission: Reaching Out from Within, Inc. is a self-help program for inmates in Kansas correctional facilities. The program is designed for incarcerated men and women who desire to make changes in their behavior that enable them to become role models for nonviolence while in correctional facilities and productive family members and citizens upon return to the community. These men and women run weekly meetings using curriculum written by inmates that teach life skills and helps them make positive changes in their lives and helps break the cycle of violence. The GED program at Lansing Correctional facility is run by committed volunteers with assistance from several well-educated inmate group members. Those who obtain their GED while in prison are likely to return and are better able to find employment upon release from prison. As of September 2014, ROFW volunteers have individually mentored 57 offenders, 40 have been out of prison more than six months and no longer receive formal mentoring, 12 are still inside the prison and have not yet been released, 1 is in the first six months following release and 4 were dropped from the program prior to their release. Of the 40 mentees who have been out of prison for more than six months, only one has returned to prison for a new charge and 4 were brought back to prison for 60-90 days due to a technical violation of special provision of their parole plans. These results are significantly better than the usual recidivism rate of the general prison population in Kansas.

name: LIFT THEM UP INTERNATIONAL
mission: Child Sponsorship Program: We currently have 51 orphans and other vulnerable children, from 4 different cities, connected with US-based Sponsors. For $40 per month, through this relationship, the children have been given an education, healthcare, food, clothes, shoes, monthly hygiene supplies, Bible teaching, beds, blankets, mosquito nets, and wash tubs. We want to set them up for success at home, school, and in life. They also receive private tutoring, throughout the week, to help them get caught up in school; and warm meals, served at their local church, each Saturday. Several kilos of dried food are sent home with them each month, so that their families can have something to eat, too. We started sending food home with the kids, because we were finding out that many would only get to eat once every 4 days and the 'meals' that they were receiving at school were insufficient.; Nutrition Program: We've served over 20,000 meals to the malnourished children of a village in the Nyaraguru region of Rwanda, in the southern part of the country. This began, because many of the children in our sponsorship program, were too weak to go to school, even if they got sponsored. So we started serving meals to those children. Our Nutrition Program now serves over 800 children and has created 11 part-time jobs in this village. It has truly changed the lives of these little ones and restored hope, in a once hopeless situation. Meals for the children consist of: meat, beans, cabbage, and rice or a cup of porridge (hot oat meal and milk), and a gummy vitamin. On average, each $1 USD donated, provides one meal of each of those, so $1=2 meals. Our hope is to be able to provide 4 months of regular meals, served 5 days a week; Widow Blessings Program: For only $50, our donors can bless widows with a 20lb bag of corn flour, 20lbs of rice, and 1 gallon of cooking oil- this will provide the average family with 3 months of food. So far, 13 widows and their families, located across Rwanda, have received these gifts. It has been a huge blessing to the women who receive them, the churches who distribute them, and the donors, who receive a picture of the woman whose family they have blessed.

name: HONORING OUR VETERANS
mission: Photography Program:The goal of the photography session is to teach the veterans to view life from a different perspective and to open their mind to the beauty that surrounds them. The photography session encompasses many aspects of photography such as classroom instruction on exposure, lighting, night-time photography, and printing, etc. With the assistance of volunteer photography instructors, the veterans travel to various areas including Grand Teton and Yellowstone National Park s to photograph nature, wildlife, mountains, rivers, sunrises, and sunsets. Near the end of the session, each of the veterans choose a few of their favorite photos to print, matte and take home.; Fly Casting and Fly Tying Instruction & Fly Fishing Trips:The Fly Fishing Therapy Session encompasses all aspects of fly fishing with fly casting instruction, a fly tying class and workshop, education on river stewardship and the etymology of our region, and fly fishing trips on the beautiful rivers, lakes, and tributaries in Jackson Hole. This session provides the opportunity for each veteran to connect with nature in a very peaceful environment. The skill and art of casting a fly is mentally therapeutic for the veterans as well as requiring focus on the use of gross motor skills. The fly tying education encourages a deep level of focus and concentration as well as challenging fine motor skills.; Hunting Sessions:The Elk and Antelope Hunt Therapy Sessions are made possible through the use of Wyoming Statue 32-1-705 (k), which authorizes the holder of any valid big game license to surrender said license to the department for reissuance to a veteran with disabilities, as established by the commission rule and regulation, selected and sponsored by a nonprofit charitable organization providing hunting opportunities for disabled veterans. We are grateful to have landowners and locals who wish to donate their elk and antelope hunting tags to our disabled veterans, and a dedicated team of experienced guides and outfitters that ensure a memory of a lifetime. Additionally, the organization provides for the processing and shipping of meat from the hunt to the veterans and their family.; Reunion:The Reunion session was very unique situation. Four Veterans who served together in Afghanistan had attended a previous session. The session proved to be very therapeutic due to the commonalities. One of the Veterans lost his wife a few months earlier to cancer. His depression began to overpower him. It was suggested that we have the reunion session in an attempt to assist this Veteran with his grief and depression. We made a special allowance for this session and allowed spouses and children to attend hoping to help his 3 children deal with their grief as well. name: SCOPE-SCIENCE AND CITIZENS ORGANIZED FOR PURPOSE AND EXPLORATION
mission: In 2017, SCOPE continued to increase and develop its national presence, which brought greater opportunities and resources to families, students, adults and SCOPE partners. SCOPE strengthened partnerships with the Arizona based program Chief Science Officers (CSO). Additionally, SCOPE grew its involvement with The United State Navy and Air Force, to share access and outcomes along the STEM Education to Workforce pathway. Together, SCOPE and partners brought education to teens, industry, education, legislative and community stakeholders. A focus centered on undeserved, underrepresented, and the public at large.SCOPE, again, expanded its Festival within a Festival model at Fair St. Louis, over the 4th of July holiday, (serving over 250,000) and Taste of STL (serving 125,000) with partners representing informal and formal education and workforce. This resulted in over ~25,000 being served directly with interactive STEAM experiences. CSO students were also trained to bring this model to their schools and community. This gave them the ability to teach what they learned, deepen their understanding of STEAM, along with encourage their peers to do the same. Hands on experiences in engineering, biotechnology, physics, math were delivered. The Air Force virtual 3D was augmented with SCOPE providing goggles to fairgoers, so the experience would continue post event. Navy brought SeaPerch underwater robotics and the program is being sought by Tennessee CSOs. To facilitate entering the pipeline, SCOPE again brought both the financial aid representatives from MOST 529, as well as the St Louis Career Center. To deepen understanding, SCOPE created a video from the events to share with SCOPE followers, the public, stakeholders, and media. A robust social media campaign increased traffic to SCOPE, partners and events.As in previous years, loyal STEAM partners from Indiana and Kansas City traveled to highlight the strong STEAM leadership of public universities, industry and informal STEAM programs. Their programs and offerings continue to be highlighted on our scopenational.org website.SCOPE presented the Chief Science Officer program to donors, educators, and industry. It was met with great response by KWS, Toyota, St Louis Community College Plant & Life Sciences, University of Missouri Kansas, Challenger Learning Center, St Louis, Indiana and Tennessee public schools. Together, they joined with SCOPE in an inaugural CSO Institute. This focused on understanding opportunities, connecting with resources and training how to bring the information to peers, and community. 20 STEM/STEAM CSO Ambassadors were in this first class and the CSO Institute was met with great response and outcomes. Students returned to their areas to outreach at their schools, at local events and to their community School Boards and Chambers. SCOPE was instrumental in bringing an application for St Louis, MO to become a recognized STEM Ecosystem in the national network. The designation was granted in the fourth quarter of 2017 and SCOPE became one of the lead founding partners. At the Kansas City National Conference, SCOPE presented it's model to others and created the framework for future collaborative efforts. Collaborations continued with University of Central Missouri, University of Missouri Kansas City, St Louis Community College, Missouri Western University, 4-H, Navy, Toyota Bodine, BioSTL, Cortex,, BERDST, Girl Scouts, Arizona Tech Council, and more are invaluable, yet often what they offer is unknown. Through numerous events, meetings, website and social media activities, SCOPE insures resources and outreach are continually used for the strongest lasting STEAM outcomes.

mission: COMPASSSION & EDUCATION ... Organized and hosted MLD Family Conference(tm) in Plymouth Meeting, PA with 76 people in attendance. Brought together families, researchers, doctors, service providers and other resources for two-day meetings with the common goal of providing insight to improving the quality of life for those with MLD and their caregivers. We share research and clinical trial updates, answer questions, and allocate the bulk of the time to facilitating the building relationships between the families. (approx 30 families directly affected - hundreds more when they view the live webcast and conference videos freely posted on the MLD Foundation website). Visited numerous other families in their hometowns during our other travels.; INFLUENCE RESEARCH & AWARENESS - Attended medical and scientific conferences including the NIH/RDCRN-Lysosomal Disease Network's WORLD meeting, facilitated and attended GLIA meeting, visited the FDA, NIH, NINDS, World RARE Disease Day events in DC, HHS/NICHD Newborn Screening meetings, organized two RUSP Roundtable meetings (newborn screening policy and technology), continued MLD newborn screening pilot study, transferred a set of mice from the US MLD mouse colony that we established to a new biotech firm, and visited researchers at their home facilities representing the interests of MLD families and other researchers. Supported global clinical trial recruiting and development of MLD standards of care. Working towards standards for clinical research excellence to improve quality of life for patients/families and further lysosomal and leukodystrophy research.; COMPASSION ... MLD Family Compassion Fund(tm) and Compassion grants support many families. Meet with families and small family groups where a MLD Family Conference is not possible. These visits and Third Program Service Accomplishments Description MLD Family Gatherings(tm) bring families in a geography together to meet each other - often for the very first time to educate and further connect those families with the MLD Foundation and other families. We share research and clinical trial updates, answer questions, and allocate the bulk of the time to building relationships between the families. (approx 20 families). Direct Quality of Life case management for several families. Direct family financial support through our independently managed MLD Family Compassion Fund.; COMPASSION & RESEARCH - PATIENT POWERED SUPPORT AND RESEARCH ... The MLD Family Discussion List is the world's largest electronic gathering of families affected by MLD. They share experiences, compassion, support, and ideas with each other to provide the highest quality of life to those affected by MLD. Partnered with Genetic Alliance on a PCORI funded patient powered research network which will result in a next generation registry launch to supplement the MLD Family Profile registry which captures family demographic information and is quickly becoming the largest international database of MLD family histories. This data will be compiled and shared in a de-identified manner to improve MLD research, natural history studies, and clinical trials. Also includes electronic and paper publications. (700+ families); EDUCATION ... Visited NIH, FDA, Capitol Hill to educate on issues of importance to MLD affected families, researchers, and industry. World RARE disease day events, FDA rare disease workshops, HHS/ACHDNC (newborn screening) testimony. Focus on the implementation of electronic medical records, orphan disease research, registries, and newborn screening for rare diseases. Host numerous websites to inform, educate, influence, and support MLD families and research.; Rare Honor/Gifting With Purpose ... licensed patent and supporting implementation of fund raising platform for MLD Foundation. Have rights to make available to all 501c3s with a royalty stream to MLD Foundation.

name: STOCKTON HISTORICAL MARITIME MUSEUM INC
mission: The Stockton Maritime Museum had another year of growth and accomplishments in 2017. Our actively participating adult volunteer corps has continued to grow, with 4 new participants regularly attending our workparties. The Discovery Challenge Academy sent us 8 cadets to each workparty, along with one instructor. And over 100 Building Futures Academy students have completed their community service requirements by participating in the restoration process. Major projects completed during the year include the radio room, ships office, laundry, and Combat Information Center, or CIC, and reconstruction of the watertight bulkhead between the forward and aft engine rooms. Ongoing major projects are forward berthing compartment reconstruction, and watertight hatch reconstruction and installation on level 1. Final watertight treatment on -01 level was also substantially completed in 2017. Eight hearty volunteers attended the Bremerton Naval Shipyard annual Open House in July. We recovered several tons of needed parts and supplies from decommissioned navy ships destined for the scrap yard. It is our museum's most important source of authentic navy ship parts. Three museum directors attended the annual Historic Naval Ships Association, HNSA, conference in Charleston, SC, held aboard the historic WWII aircraft carrier USS Yorktown. Topics discussed at the conference covered marketing, fundraising, restoration techniques, STEM education opportunities, and how to remain relevant in our local communities. The year ended with an appreciation dinner and party for all volunteers, directors and some local supporters. Video presentations were made highlighting the year's progress, and volunteer Jack Frost was presented with a restoration award from the HNSA.

name: FOR THE FISHES
mission: 1.EDUCATION AND OUTREACH: FOR THE FISHES (FTF) ADVOCATES FOR THE END OF THE CAPTURE, PURCHASE, AND DISPLAY OF WILD MARINE LIFE IN PERSONAL SALTWATER AQUARIUMS. ACTIVITIES INCLUDE BUT ARE NOT LIMITED TO PUBLIC ENGAGEMENT AND ADVOCACY, COALITION BUILDING, AND EFFORTS AIMED AT REDUCING CONSUMER DEMAND FOR WILD MARINE LIFE. A)HAWAII OUTREACH & EDUCATION: HAWAII'S COMPARATIVELY SMALL CORAL REEFS ARE THE WORLD'S THIRD LARGEST SOURCE OF REEF FISHES AND OTHER CREATURES FOR THE GLOBAL AQUARIUM TRADE SUPPLYING MARINE ANIMALS TO HOBBYISTS AND BUSINESSES, ALIKE. AN UNLIMITED NUMBER OF MARINE ANIMALS ARE ALLOWED TO BE TAKEN. IN 2016, THE TRADE IN HAWAII CAPTURED AT LEAST 565,749 MARINE ANIMALS, AN AMOUNT SEVERAL TIMES HIGHER THAN TYPICALLY TAKEN FROM AUSTRALIA'S ENTIRE GREAT BARRIER REEF WHICH IS 300 TIMES LARGER THAN HAWAII'S REEF AREA. IN THE AREAS WHERE THE HAWAII TRADE OPERATES, UNLIMITED TAKE HAS DEPLETED HEAVILY TARGETED SPECIES BY UPWARDS OF 90%. FTF HAS LONG ADVOCATED FOR THE NEED FOR BETTER MANAGEMENT AND SOLUTIONS, INCLUDING AN END TO HAWAII'S CORAL REEF WILDLIFE TRADE. IN A 2017 HAWAII SUPREME COURT RULING, TOGETHER WITH CO-PLAINTIFFS, WE PREVAILED IN A YEARS' LONG STRATEGY TO BRING HAWAII'S MARINE AQUARIUM TRADE INTO COMPLIANCE WITH HAWAII'S ENVIRONMENTAL POLICY ACT. IN OCTOBER 2017, PERMITS THAT HAD BEEN ISSUED FOR OVER 40 YEARS TO CAPTURE MARINE LIFE FOR AQUARIUM PURPOSES WERE DEEMED ILLEGAL AND INVALID UNTIL PROPER ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW HAS BEEN COMPLETED. AS A RESULT OF A LONG TERM FTF STRATEGY, HAWAII RESIDENTS ARE MORE AWARE OF THE IMPACTS OF THE MARINE AQUARIUM TRADE TO HAWAII'S CORAL REEFS AND WILDLIFE. AN ASSESSMENT OF THE EFFECTS OF ONGOING EDUCATION AND OUTREACH EFFORTS DETERMINED THAT 83% OF HAWAII RESIDENTS SUPPORT ENDING THE CAPTURE OF HAWAII'S REEF WILDLIFE BY THE GLOBAL MARINE AQUARIUM TRADE. FTF IS WORKING WITH MAJOR CORPORATIONS TO REDUCE THE EXPORT AND SALE OF HAWAII'S MARINE LIFE FOR THE GLOBAL AQUARIUM HOBBY. AN APPEAL FROM FTF TO EBAY RESULTED IN IMPLEMENTATION OF A BAN ON EBAY TROPICAL FISH LISTINGS OF MARINE LIFE CAPTURED IN HAWAII. AN FTF APPEAL TO ALASKA AIRLINES RESULTED IN AN EMBARGO ON THE CARRIAGE OF HAWAII'S REEF WILDLIFE ABOARD ITS PLANES DEPARTING HAWAII. B)TANK WATCH: MOST PEOPLE ARE UNAWARE THAT FEWER THAN 5% OF THE FISH SPECIES KEPT IN SALTWATER AQUARIUMS CAN BE AQUACULTURED ON A COMMERCIAL SCALE, OR THAT THE U.S. MARINE AQUARIUM TRADE ANNUALLY IMPORTS OVER 11 MILLION WILD CORAL REEF FISHES FOR AQUARIUM HOBBYISTS, SMALL BUSINESS AND LARGE PUBLIC DISPLAY AQUARIUMS. FOR THE FISHES ADVOCATES FOR AN END TO THE KEEPING OF WILD MARINE LIFE IN PERSONAL SALTWATER AQUARIUMS AND WORKS TO EDUCATE CONSUMERS AND THE PUBLIC IN ORDER TO REDUCE CONSUMER DEMAND FOR THIS WILDLIFE. IN 2017 WE REACHED AQUARIUM HOBBYISTS AND THOSE INTERESTED IN MARINE FISHKEEPING THROUGH OUR MOBILE APP, VIDEO VIEWS AND MARKET RESEARCH WITH A SURVEY INSTRUMENT THAT WAS ALSO GEARED TOWARD EDUCATION. TANK WATCH - THE GOOD FISH / BAD FISH TOOL FOR SALTWATER AQUARIUMS WAS DOWNLOADED 9,526 TIMES. USER RETENTION, THE NUMBER OF USERS WHO CONTINUED TO USE THE APP AFTER FIRST USE, WAS FIVE TIMES GREATER THAN OTHER EDUCATIONAL MOBILE APPS 30 DAYS AFTER DOWNLOAD. AT 90 DAYS POST DOWNLOAD, USER RETENTION STILL OUTPACED OTHER EDUCATIONAL APPS. OUR THREE EDUCATIONAL VIDEOS, RANGING IN LENGTH FROM 1 - 3.5 MINUTES IN LENGTH EACH, WERE VIEWED OVER 125,000 TIMES FOR OVER 59,000 MINUTES ON FACEBOOK AND YOUTUBE. WE EDUCATED OVER 1,000 ADDITIONAL AQUARIUM HOBBYISTS THROUGH MARKET RESEARCH AND GAINED A BETTER UNDERSTANDING OF HOBBYIST FISH PURCHASING BEHAVIOR TO BETTER INFORM OUR OUTREACH EFFORTS.; CONSERVATION: FOR THE FISHES WORKS TO CONSERVE CORAL REEF WILDLIFE THROUGH REDUCING ILLEGAL, UNREPORTED AND UNREGULATED FISHING IN THE MARINE AQUARIUM TRADE. ACTIVITIES INCLUDE, BUT ARE NOT LIMITED TO, ADVOCACY, RESEARCH, AND CITIZEN ENGAGEMENT IN DOCUMENTING AND REPORTING SUSPECTED ILLEGAL ACTIVITIES IN THE MARINE AQUARIUM TRADE. A)CYANIDE FISH ASSESSMENT: EXPERTS ESTIMATE THAT UPWARDS OF 90% OF CORAL REEF FISHES SOLD IN THE MARINE AQUARIUM TRADE ARE ILLEGALLY CAPTURED WITH CYANIDE WHICH IS USED TO PARALYZE FISH FOR EASY CAPTURE. CYANIDE IS HIGHLY POISONOUS TO BOTH THE VERTEBRATE AND INVERTEBRATE ORGANISMS EXPOSED TO IT: AT HIGHER CONCENTRATIONS IT IS IMMEDIATELY LETHAL, AND AT LOWER CONCENTRATIONS IT CAUSES ORGAN AND TISSUE DAMAGE THAT ARE IRREVERSIBLE AND LEAD TO DELAYED MORTALITY. FTF IS WORKING WITH A LEADING CORAL EXPERT AND FORENSIC ECOTOXICOLOGIST IN RESEARCH TO ASSESS THE PREVALENCE OF CYANIDE- CAUGHT FISH IN THE U.S. MARINE AQUARIUM TRADE. IN 2017 WE CONTINUED TESTING MARINE FISHES PURCHASED THROUGH U.S. WHOLESALERS AND RETAILERS.

name: MV GATE INC
mission: In support of its objectives, during 2017 MVGATE continued and expanded its core mission to help Marin parents and communities provide advanced learning opportunities to children who desire and need more educational challenges than traditional schooling provides. It directly provided evening and after school enrichment programs to some 2,000 children at 15 schools through Marin County. In 2017 MVGATE-Core added an advanced Computer Science summer program, which served 30 middle school and high school kids in a week-long intensive programming class. In 2017 MVGATE-Core added a new advanced math program that allowed 50 middle school students to participate in Marin's first open session of the American Mathematics Competition.; In 2017 MVGATE's new program, Family Code Night (FCN), shared best practices pioneered in Marin with communities around the US and world. FCN helps schools offer their own Family Code Nights and related K-8 computer science learning programs. It has been featured on the front page of the Sunday New York Times, on the White House website, and at the 2016 White House Computer Science for All Summit. The program can be run by any school, in English or in Spanish, with no special resources or training, and at virtually no expense to the school, using an FCN Event Kit created and provided for free by MVGATE. Thousands of Event Kits have been distributed to principals and educators, and hundreds of Family Code Nights have been held for tens of thousands of participants. During 2017 MVGATE-FCN delivered professional training and services to public school districts including Norfolk VA (33,000 students) and Chicago IL (361,000 students).

name: CENTER FOR DIGITAL ARCHAEOLOGY
mission: We work with archaeologists to go paperless and adopt tools to workflows that save time, paper, and money in the field and in post-processing. We do this by using Codifi, an archaeological data and media management solution that integrates data and media generated by excavation and survey into one digital database. Codifi was developed as a collaboration between CoDA and Codifi, Inc. in more than three years of development led by Chief Technology Officer Michael Ashley, with a team of five high level professional developers, data architects, and UI designers. After two years of testing by over 40 professional archaeologists, in 6 different projects, over 18 field seasons, Codifi is now ready to help all archaeology professionals. Codifi replaces and augments paper based recording and rapidly accelerates data entry while providing a solid born-archival workflow for documents, images, video and geo-spatial information.

name: BENTON FRANKLIN COMMUNITY HEALTH ALLIANCE
mission: Building on the 2016 Community Health Needs Assessment, the Alliance adopted and published the 2017 Community Health Improvement Plan, which addresses Access to Care, Obesity and Diabetes, and adds Behavioral Health as a third important community health need. The Health Access Team continued to expand its knowledge and understanding of emerging trends in health care, and available community resources. This is accomplished on an ongoing basis through guest presentations at monthly meetings. The information gathered is subsequently used to inform the Alliance and several of its subcommittees.; The Oral Health Coalition (OHC) is committed to educating medical and dental professionals on the importance of integrating dental and physical health care. The Oral Health Coalition produces the annual Eastern Washington Medical-Dental Summit, for clinicians of both disciplines. The summit features practical clinical applications informed by the latest research to enable physicians and dentists to improve patient care and community health. The Committee is also working to increase the number of dentists practicing within Federally Qualified Health Centers. This need is an ongoing priority.The Oral Health Coalition recommendedand the Alliance acceptedintegration of Oral Health with Mental and Physical health care. The Oral Health Coalition produced the fourth of its successful Medical-Dental Summits, this one focused on airway management involving dentistry and physical health. More than 200 attended this two-day event.; Active since 1997, the Tri-Cities Diabetes Coalition serves the Southeastern portion of Washington State. Activities include community events to promote awareness of risk factors, prevention strategies, and management and control of diabetes. The mission of the annual Tri-Cities Diabetes Coalition Fair is to implement diabetes education awareness.; The Behavioral Health (nee Mental Health) Committee began preparation of a brochure which is focused on reducing the stigma attached to mental health care. It has also closely monitored developments associated with changes in the bi-county mental health system regarding people who receive care through Medicaid, which is moving toward bi-directional integration of Mental and Physical health care.; The Tri-Cities Patient Safety Coalition continued its investigation of hospital readmission rates, which are highest in the State. Findings included communication gaps between hospital and skilled nursing, and between clinical settings and community organizations. Another key factor was thought to be a lack of community understanding about availability and desirability of end-of-life care. A Transitions subcommittee was formed to address the communication issues, achieving some early success.; A new End-of-Life subcommittee was formed, and has begun holding dinner meetings to discuss ways to improve community use of various tools to encourage end-of-life preference discussions among families and caregivers. The subcommittee is seeking to learn about best practices from across the region.; The Greater Columbia Accountable Community of Health (ACH) achieved independent status early in 2017, with the Alliances Executive Director moving full-time to the ACH, which is a nine-county and the Yakama Nation version of the Alliance funded by the State Health Care Authority using Medicaid Transition Demonstration funds. The Alliance will work closely with the ACH to address priority community health issues.

Funding is used for supplies to have public workshops to teach the art for the event and teach the history.; Education: We have offer our space to provide historical education opportunitise to the community. Some classes are simple tutoring sessions and others include self care classes.; Recreation: This is a core aspect of our efforts. We have an open youth full basketball court. We have open weight rooms. This is community lead recreation activities. We also have Danza Azteca once a week, Ballet Folklorico twice a week, and we have Judo twice a week. These recreation programs have served nearly 300 people this year.

name: PACIFIC PALISADES TASK FORCE ON HOMELESSNESS

The PPTFH has raised significant funds to support these service efforts.; ENFORCEMENT COORDINATION: The PPTFH Enforcement Coordination Team has partnered with the local police and fire departments to ensure that local laws are enforced, particularly those to related to neighborhood safety. Additionally, this year the Enforcement Coordination Team has initiated extensive homeless camp clean up operation in fire zones where camps are prohibited. The team has cleaned up over 60 campsites.; EDUCATION: THE PPTFH continues to sponsor bimonthly, interactive community meetings on various topics related to homelessness. Topics have included: veterans, PTSD and what we can do to help, responses to panhandling, service resistant homeless in the Palisades, how to talk to our children about homelessness, supportive housing options for homeless and success stories of individuals who have been moved off the streets into housing.. The entire Palisades community, including its homeless residents have benefited from the work of the PPTFH and its partners.

name: CHINA - US ENERGY EFFICIENCY ALLIANCE
mission: The Alliance continues to connect energy leaders to share common problems and catalyze solutions to fight climate change. We organized a panel of top experts to discuss the topic, "The Future of Electric Buses in the U.S. and China." Energy leaders on the panel included the EV and infastructure experts from PG&E, SCE, BYD, the world's largest EV manufacturer and is based in China, the head of CALSTART and the director of the China Center for Energy and Transportation at the University of California, Davis. About 30 people attended from a range of backgrounds--business, academia and government. A reporter from E&E News wrote a story about our panel. The Alliance organized a second panel of top experts to discuss the topic, "The Utilities of the Future in the U.S. and China." These energy leaders represented PG&E, NRDC, National Renewable Energy Laboratory, Regulatory Assistance Project, and the Paulson Institute. It was attended by a diverse group of about 30 representatives from the public and private sectors. the Alliance also facilitated educational exchanges between Chinese and American experts in electric vehicles and power management known as demand response. Under a contract with NRDC, the Alliance identified EV and DR experts from the U.S. utilities to travel to China to share best practices and to learn the state of China's development in this area. Utilities in both countries face common problems in integrating electric vehciles and renewable energy into a smarter grid. The Alliance organized a pilot workshop in partnership with PG&E to educate Chinese real estate developers with properties in the Bay Area how to save energy in their buildings, which include commercial and multi-story residential properties.

name: FRIENDS OF IRISH STUDIES IN THE WEST
mission: The Friends fully funded the Irish dance courses taught at the University of Montana [UM] in the spring and fall of 2017. The Irish dance program continues to attract a large number of students. The dance is currently studying for full certification, which will enable her to organize and adjudicate dance competitions as well as qualify her to develop a recognized and accredited curriculum of courses in Irish dance. The Friends provided a substantial amount of funding to bring an Irish language and an Irish music instructor to campus for the fall of 2017 and the spring of 2018. The support for the music instructor enabled the Irish Studies program to promote and offer a course in Irish Music and Song in the spring of 2018.The Friends sponsored a speakers program in the fall of 2017. Micheline Sheehy Skeffington gave public lectures in Butte and Missoula in October and November 2017; Dr. Ruan ODonnell gave public lectures in Missoula, Butte and Kalispell in December 2017. The Friends sponsored the Irish Christmas program which comprised two public concerts of Irish music, song and dance. The performers from the Irish language and Irish dance classes were joined by musicians from the student body on campus and from the community. Both shows were a great success. The Friends also supported the Irish Language Study Abroad program in Ireland. Their support enabled less-well-off students to avail of this opportunity. This was the Study Abroad Irish Language immersion program in west Kerry, Ireland. There were 19 students enrolled for the course in 2017. The Friends also remained very active in promoting Irish culture in the community in other ways. In March of 2017, the group organized a St. Patricks Day celebration supported by over 300 people, drawing many from outlying areas such as Hamilton, Anaconda, Helena, Butte and Great Falls.The Friends also organized a week-long Irish language immersion course in Butte. A total of 19 students from Montana, California, Colorado, Washington and Oregon participated in the course. This is one of only two offered in the country and it is very popular among adult learners. The Friends provided financial support for the Montana Grizzlies Hurling club. This club was established on campus to introduce students to the ancient Irish game of hurling. Friends support enabled the hurling club to buy equipment for the students. The club was very enthusiastically supported and proved to be very successful, winning the College National Hurling Championship in 2017. mission: In its first year of operation, Castaways Thrift Co. successfully took in copious amounts of donations from the community, effectively reducing excess waste in our landfills. Also, the community has been appreciative of our well-organized thrift store and the low prices we are able to provide, enabling them to "stretch" their dollar on needed clothing and household items. Profits from Castaways Thrift Co. are being sent to Solus Christus, a nearby Christian substance abuse safe-house for women seeking to enter long-term rehabilitation. Solus Christus provides a warm and loving Christian environment to these women while assisting them in the lengthy and tedious process of applying to long-term treatment programs. Many people come through the doors of Castaways Thrift looking for prayer and direction for themselves or for a loved one trapped in addiction, and it has been our great privilege to pray with them and to direct them to the help that Solus Christus humbly offers.

name: ARTS IN MOTION
mission: Dancing classrooms - a ballroom dance program, during the school day for 5th and 6th grade students as well as 9th-12th grade special education students. Dancing classrooms introduces children to the art form of ballroom dance, which they can enjoy throughout their life. Dancing classrooms is also a specific method of teaching dance that is designed to foster teamwork, mutual respect and discipline among diverse classmates. Through the mastery and performance of six basic ballroom dances, students develop a greater sense of confidence, civility, tolerance, and patience within themselves and for each other. Students improve their fitness and coordination as they focus their physical energy on the rhythmic movement to music. Finally, the students broaden their knowledge of the artistic, cultural, historic, and geographic elements of the six dances. Last year's enrollment was approximately 1,900 students.; Saturday Scholarships - an extension of dancing classrooms. Students who successfully complete the dancing classrooms program are eligible to participate in additional free classes. The program builds on the dances and lessons learned in dancing classrooms as well as fosters social awareness, confidence, and self-esteem through the practice of social dance. Last year's enrollment was approximately 275 students.; Golden Ballroom is an exercise program for the elderly who reside in long-term care facilities, incorporating intentional movement using classic ballroom dances with specific era/genre music and rhythms. We strive to provide a fun and energetic atmosphere where individuals can learn to build confidence, improve social skills, reduce stress, get much needed exercise and improve memory as many studies have shown. Last year this program included about 50 individuals.

mission: While these birds are protected, no agency support funds these activities the caring of injured birds and is often left to private charities. Annually we treat 100-150 injured wild raptors admitted from the public and state agencies in need of our medical and housing services. When we (Don and Jane Veltkamp, volunteer board members) are off- site, we hire help to care for the birds of prey in our care. These university students receive education as well as training and are offered a small stipend.Maintenance operations go on 365 days a year as we care for the up to 50 raptors, keep records, respond to emergency calls. Daily food preparation, feeding and food procurement are required for these special predatory birds of prey. Obtaining predatory the bird food supply is critical. Service accomplishments increase each year to meet public demands and birds admitted. Each year more educational birds are added to our teaching team and the request for our unique programs continues. It is yet to be determined how many children are inspired to conserve these magnificent birds of prey and how many of our rehabilitated patients returned to the wild to live along life. While intangible to predict the results, the work is so very meaningful to children and birds. Increasing requests for our unique educational programs occur each year. While impossible to predict how many children are inspired towards raptor conservation and how many raptors returned to the wild live long, it is a worthwhile mission. We also offer public tours of the facility and educate hundreds of people each year about raptor conservation. We also travel to local elementary schools and other public venues with trained live eagles, hawks, owls, falcons, and ospreys to further educate the public about raptor conservation.

name: PABLO SANDOVAL FAMILY FOUNDATION INC
mission: At 23, Sandoval used jokes about his weight as a catalyst for teaming with the American Heart Association to urge kids to stay healthy. He spoke in his native language to elementary-school-age kids at San Franciscos predominantly Hispanic Mission Cultural Center in the summer of 2010. This past season, after losing 40 pounds, Sandoval made a similar appearance with his brother and training partner Michael at St. Peter School, to the delight of Vice Principal Mercy Sister Marian Rose Power. In todays world our children need heroes and heroines to look for inspiration, she told Catholic-SF.org. Pablo and his brother did this for the children and families at St. Peters. The teachers will follow up with lessons on nutrition and exercise so it will be far more than a one-day event.When Pablo played for the Class A San Jose Giants, he lived with host family Donna and Ed Musgrave and grew close to them as they helped him adapt to a new country, culture and language. Donnas subsequent battle with bladder cancer galvanized Sandoval to do what he could to stand up for her and stand up to cancer. In October of 2010, Sandoval joined fellow World Series players in signing The Wall for Stand Up To Cancer, naming his baseball mom Donna. Its exciting to know that MLB does those things to help others, he told MLB.com. We need to give support to make good things happen. In 2013, an MLB public service announcement featuring Pablo and Dustin Pedroia introducing Stand Up to Cancers new app aired during the World Series, and Sandoval held up his phone, with the app saying My Friend Donna.In 2011, the FBI honored Sandoval for partnering with the American Football Coaches Association (AFCA)/FBI National ID Program to provide 50,000 Child ID (fingerprinting) Kits to children in the San Francisco community. Pablo is a professional athlete who understands the importance of investing back in the community that supports you, and 50,000 children in San Francisco will be safer due to his efforts, said Kenny Hansmire, the AFCA/FBI National Child ID Program executive director. Sandoval also furnished kits for families in Venezuela.Time with Pablo has become a popular request for children participating in Make-A-Wish Greater Bay Area, and he has hosted numerous Wish Kids and their families for visits to AT&T Park. During a visit to Baseball City in Scottsdale, Arizona, he took part in a free clinic for kids and also spent time with kids from that Make-A-Wish chapter.Sandoval was named as a Guest Judge for MLBs Honorary Bat Girl program for 2014 recognizing fans who have been affected by breast cancer and worked to eradicated it, raising the profile of the PINK initiative. He met with the San Francisco Giants Bat Girl before a game and escorted her to the field for the first pitch.Sandoval wears the bracelet for Until Theres A Cure, raising funds and awareness for HIV/AIDS.Pablo has spent numerous hours visiting with injured U.S. troops to lift their spirits and boost morale, in hopes of aiding in their recovery process.Sandoval has initiated Twitter and Facebook takeovers of official team media sites to interact with fans and answer their questions. He loves social media as a way of connecting with fans, and stays active on Twitter, Instagram and Facebook.Pablo has made several visits to sick kids, and a special program at UCSF Benioff Childrens Hospital in August 2013 marked the official introduction of his Pablo Sandoval Family Foundation. Pablo visited with 50 children and their families in the playroom, and then was escorted for one-on-one time with the children too sick to leave their beds. The Giants shared video footage that night with fans at a sold-out game. I just want to see those kids happy, he said that day.His foundation since has hosted 25 school children at a spring training game, and on June 1, 2014, a partnership with the San Francisco Giants Community Fund and MLB launched Win a Day with the Panda, the Ultimate Pablo Sandoval Giants Experience. Pablo donated all of the raffle proceeds to the Junior Giants and their RBI program.During the 2014 World Series, one small gesture informed the world of the big heart of Pablo Sandoval. The Royals seven-run bottom of the second inning of Game 6 lasted 33 minutes as Kansas City went to work on a lopsided victory. When it finally ended with a foul ball into the glove of Sandoval, he handed it over the railing to a kid. A kid clad in Royals blue.The cameras caught the moment, and there was a bit of a buzz on the internet as baseball fans commented on the generosity of Sandoval even in the heat of the moment.Fans in the Bay Area and Venezuela merely shrugged. They had already seen the big heart of the Panda.

mission: Annual meeting of membership - papers presented and speakers on current topics. Representing 67 of the nation's universities, the NAUFRP has focused recent efforts on a number of emerging topics. It has worked with public and private sector partners to identify and prioritize a national research agenda, and formed alliances with other non-governmental organizations on a range of issues including natural resource sustainability, renewable energy, and climate change.Sponsored the annual Family Forests Education Award with the National Woodland Owners Association. Sponsored the annual Family Forests Education Award with the National Woodland Owners Association. There was one recipient in 2017: Oregon State University. The award were presented at the NAUFRP Annual Meeting on November 15, 2017 in Albuquerque, NM.; The Executive Committee established an Ad Hoc Communications Committee chaired by Dean Mary Watzin (North Carolina State University) as part of the continued implementation of the USDA McIntire-Stennis Program Strategic Plan which the membership worked on over 2015-2016. The goals of the committee are to 1) increase brand awareness and build sufficient recognition of the value of the McIntire-Stennis program to ensure ongoing support and funding; 2)Communicate aligned and compelling stories that illustrate the value and impact of the McIntire-Stennis program across the US; and, 3) Connect the dots directly between what McIntire-Stennis funds and the many unique impacts, innovations and innovators that results of the program. A workshop was held in Atlanta in August 2017 comprised of NAUFRP members and work continued in another workshop at the NAUFRP General Assembly meeting on November 15, 2017 in Albuquerque, NM. The work will continue into 2018.In late 2017, the NAUFRP leadership communicated with the general membership encouraging them to participate in a Listening Session process by the USDA National Institute for Food and Agriculture (NIFA) on top food and agricultural (includes forestry) research, extension and education priorities the agency should address. Of the results, two forestry priorities forest health and ecosystem services were identified in the top ten responses the agency received.; The NAUFRP Executive Committee began discussions with the U.S. Endowment for Forestry and Communities and USDA Forest Service to begin implementation of recommendations by the Blue Ribbon Commission on Forest and Forest Products Research and Development. The Commission reviewed the state of research in the forest sector and produced a final report in October 2017 http://www.usendowment.org/blueribbonreport.html.Increasing diversity and inclusion within NAUFRP institutions (faculty and student body) continues to be a priority of the organization. NAUFRP has assisted the Society of American Foresters (SAF) with developing a national Diversity and Inclusion Policy, created a Diversity and Inclusion Working Group and Diversity Leadership Award. NAUFRP is discussing establishing a clearing house on academic institutions diversity efforts/actions for the associations webpage . The NAUFRP Diversity Chair participates in the annual meetings of the Minorities in Agriculture, Natural Resources and Related Sciences the 1890 (institutions) Agriculture Research Directors.The Executive Committee continued to work in 2017 to integrate and merge data that NAUFRP has collected over a two decade period on students in forestry and natural resources programs with that collected by the USDA Food and Agricultural Education System (http://www.faeis.ahnrit.vt.edu/). The lead FAEIS Project Leader met with the Committee at the November 14, 2017 meeting in Albuquerque, NM to discuss ongoing issues.The association is in the process of developing a Forest Health Initiative in collaboration with the Association of Public Land Grant University. Lead by Dean John Hayes (Colorado State University) a steering committee was established and a white paper developed and approved by both organizations outlining the structure and writing teams needed. Work will continue into 2018.

The program was also expanded to Biddeford in September of 2017.; Pecha Kucha - Pecha Kucha is a quarterly gathering of some 100 to 150 community members from a wide variety of backgrounds and creative professions, intended to provide an opportunity for structured, personal presentations of creative work and personal or professional explorations. The purpose is to encourage and inspire creative expression, allow creative professionals to meet, network and potentially collaborate, and also to showcase the hidden creativity in our communities. PechaKucha is a global activity and format, with over 800 cities around the world conducting similar events and programs. Each participating community shares videos or photos and scripts from its quarterly programs via the Internet. The format is 20 slides and 20 seconds for each slide. This creates a wonderful presentation of 6 minutes and 40 seconds and provides an audience and networking opportunity to people with good ideas. It is quick and consise to keep things upbeat and interesting.

name: CORVALLIS CLINIC FOUNDATION INC
mission: Project H.E.R.: This program continued to provide free health services (Help, Enlightenment, and Resources) in Benton, Linn and Lincoln counties of Oregon. The Navigator program was expanded in 2017 to support patients, including men, with all types of cancer. The program provides awareness, education and support for patients from the time of cancer diagnosis through survivorship, with the Navigator team, which consists of a nurse navigator, outreach coordinator, and cancer survivors who mentor patients free of charge with the guidance of the nurse navigator. Project H.E.R. added 82 new patients in 2017 and served a total of 740 patients. There were 17 active mentors during the year. The program started a private Facebook group for female cancer survivors in the community and a monthly e-newsletter. The MammaCare program's nurses and clinicians provided a breast/cervical cancer screening event that served 36 patients. The Cook for Cancer program provided 216 meals, or 864 servings, for families of patients who were undergoing chemotherapy treatments of all types of cancer diagnoses, oncology and hematology. Project H.E.R. nurses and clinicians also participated in other outreach events to increase awareness of breast cancer prevention and Project H.E.R. support, including (1) facilitation of "Look Good Feel Better" classes through the American Cancer Society; (2) partnership with Pink Sistas, Inc. to provide a breast cancer retreat (attended by 8 women); (3) sponsorship and tabling at the Soroptimist International Walk for the Cause event; (4) sponsorship and attendance at the annual local Soroptimist International tea and auction; and (5) support at numerous Dam Cancer (Pink Out) athletic events held at the local university and high schools. In addition to $49,648 of cash expenditures paid for programming and outreach (which includes $41,067 paid for a leased employee and $1,000 for grants), $72,749 of donated meals, services and facilities were received in 2017 for Project H.E.R. programs.; Emergency Assistance Grants: 11 individuals received emergency assistance grants ranging from $161 to $1,854 each to help them through financial hardships. These grants, paid directly to vendors such as banks, landlords, insurance companies, funeral homes, car repair shops, and utility companies, supported the individuals' medical care, basic human needs such as rent or mortgage payments and utility bills, car repair, car loan payments, funeral expenses and other expenses that the individuals were unable to pay on account of their medical illnesses, deaths in the family, or other unforeseen family circumstances.; Support of Under-served Populations: The Foundation forwarded individual donations totaling $888 to local nonprofit organizations: United Way of Benton, Linn and Lincoln counties; and Community Outreach Inc., a nonprofit organization that provides a homeless shelter, with a mission to stabilize individuals in crisis, feed the hungry, house the homeless, heal the sick, and counsel the mentally ill and substance-addicted. In addition, the Foundation awarded a $5,000 grant and forwarded individual donations of $1,500 to the local Dr. Ken & Dot Johnson Center for Youth Excellence that is being built by the local Boys & Girls Club to support youth with the goal of reducing persistent barriers that contribute to generational poverty. The center has planned to provide programming space for up to 300 teens on a daily basis and to provide nearly 2,000 local low-income youth and families with medical and mental health services. The Center's programs will aim to support the Club's 100% graduation goals for at-risk teens, provide job skills training, apprenticeships and first-time employment experiences.; Health Education Scholarships, Grants, and Lecture Series: Scholarships totaling $3,000, ranging from $500 to $1,000 each, were awarded to 4 high school and university students who are pursuing careers as doctors, nurses, physician assistants, nurse practitioners, phlebotomists, and other medical professionals. The Foundation provided a $1,500 grant to the local hospital foundation for its Asbury Lectureship series, which was attended by area physicians, nurses and other practitioners working in the area of women's health. The focus of the 2017 lectures was on obstetrics, with speakers covering the topics of opioid use and abuse in pregnancy, marijuana use in pregnancy and genetic testing, and addiction medicine.

name: TRAILS UTAH
mission: GRIT MILL CLIMBING TRAIL PROJECT - IN 2017 TRAILS UTAH CONDUCTED THE SECOND PHASE OF THE GRIT MILL CLIMBING TRAIL PROJECT IN COORDINATION WITH OUR PARTNERS THE SALT LAKE CLIMBERS ALLIANCE AND THE SALT LAKE RANGER DISTRICT OF THE UINTA-WASATCH-CACHE NATIONAL FOREST. IN THIS PHASE WE CONTRACTED WITH A PROFESSIONAL TRAIL BUILDING COMPANY, SINGLETRACK TRAILS, BASED IN COLORADO TO HELP US CONSTRUCT APPROXIMATELY .6 MILES OF A TRAIL THROUGH EXCEEDINGLY STEEP, ROUGH, ROCKY TERRAIN. WHILE ABOUT A THIRD OF THE WORK WAS ABLE TO BE ACCOMPLISHED USING A SPECIALIZED MINI-EXCAVATOR, THE REMAINDER HAD TO BE DONE BY HAND. THE WORK DONE BY HAND INVOLVED MOVING MANY LARGE GRANITE ROCKS INTO PLACE TO CREATE STAIRS AND HARDENED TRAIL SURFACES. THE RESULT IS A STUNNINGLY WELL-CRAFTED TRAIL THAT CONNECTS THE PREVIOUS YEAR'S ALPENBOCH LOOP TRAIL WITH AN AREA UP CANYON THAT WILL EVENTUALLY BECOME A PARKING AREA AND UPPER ACCESS FOR THE GRIT MILL CLIMBING AREA.; DESOLATION TRAIL REHABILITATION PROJECT - COMPLETION OF THE DESOLATION TRAIL REHABILITATION PROJECT WAS ALSO ACHIEVED IN 2017. THIS PROJECT INVOLVED THE REHABILITATION, AND IN SOME PLACES RE-ESTABLISHMENT, A HIKING TRAIL WITHIN THE MT. OLYMPUS WILDERNESS AREA OF THE UINTA-WASATCH-CACHE NATIONAL FOREST. THE LENGTH OF THE ENTIRE PROJECT WAS ALMOST NINE MILES. THE SECTION COMPLETED IN 2017 WAS APPROXIMATELY 2.7 MILES AND EXTENDED FROM PORTER PASS, ACCESSED THROUGH MILLCREEK CANYON, AND EXTENDED SOUTHWEST TO THAYNE'S CANYON. TRAILS UTAH APPLIED FOR A GRANT THROUGH UTAH STATE PARK'S RECREATIONAL TRAIL PROGRAM AND WAS ABLE TO MATCH FUNDS FROM SALT LAKE COUNTY TO GET THIS IMPORTANT BACKCOUNTRY TRAIL PROJECT COMPLETED. CREWS FROM THE UTAH CONSERVATION CORPS WERE HIRED TO DO THE WORK WHICH INVOLVED PACKING IN TOOLS, CAMPING GEAR AND SUPPLIES TO REMOTE LOCATIONS ALONG THE ROUTE. WATER WAS GENEROUSLY PACKED IN WITH THE HELP OF UTAH'S BACKCOUNTRY HORSEMEN.; MINERAL FORK TRAIL PROJECT - TRAILS UTAH PARTNERED WITH THE SALT LAKE RANGER DISTRICT (SLRD) AND UTAH STATE PARKS IN 2017 TO REOPEN THE MINERAL FORK TRAIL IN BIG COTTONWOOD CANYON (SL COUNTY), WHICH HAD BEEN CLOSED DUE TO ROCK FALL. THIS TRAIL IS IMPORTANT TO THE SLRD AND UTAH STATE PARKS AS IT IS THE ONLY TRAIL IN THE CENTRAL WASATCH THAT IS OPEN TO MOTORIZED TRAVEL. TRAILS UTAH PROVIDED FUNDING TO THE FS TO HELP DRILL AND BLAST HANGING BOULDERS AND ROCK DEBRIS AND HIRED SKYLINE CONTRACTORS TO COME UP WITH EARTH MOVING EQUIPMENT TO REMOVE THE DEBRIS PILE, RE- ESTABLISH THE TRAIL TREAD AND STABILIZE THE SLOPE ABOVE AND BELOW THE IMPROVED TRAIL.; FOOTHILL TRAIL SYSTEM - TRAILS UTAH ALSO SAW SUCCESS IN 2017 IN THE AREA OF PLANNING. GRANT MONEY RAISED THROUGH A LOCAL FOUNDATION ENABLED TU TO CONDUCT A YEAR OF STAKEHOLDER MEETINGS THAT BROUGHT TOGETHER THE UNIVERSITY OF UTAH, UTAH STATE PARKS, SALT LAKE CITY MUNICIPAL, THE STATE'S PRIMARY LAND CONSERVATION ORGANIZATION, UTAH OPEN LANDS, AND NUMEROUS OTHER INTERESTED PARTIES TO CREATE A SHARED VISION FOR A FOOTHILL TRAIL SYSTEM RUNNING NORTH TO SOUTH THROUGH THE NORTH EASTERN FOOTHILLS OF THE SALT LAKE VALLEY. BECAUSE OF THE CONSENSUS THAT WAS DEVELOPED THROUGH THE PROCESS SALT LAKE CITY STEPPED FORWARD AND COMMITTED TO FUNDING A COMPREHENSIVE TRAIL MASTER PLANNING EFFORT WITH HIRED PROFESSIONAL PLANNERS. THAT PLAN, WHICH INVOLVED SIGNIFICANT COMMUNITY INPUT, HAS SINCE BEEN COMPLETED AND WAS RECENTLY APPROVED AND FUNDED BY THE SALT LAKE CITY COUNCIL. THIS NEW TRAIL SYSTEM WILL ADD 73 MILES OF TRAIL TO THE EXISTING TRAIL SYSTEM, CREATE SEVERAL NEW TRAILHEADS, PUT A NEEDED MANAGEMENT PROGRAM IN PLACE AND BECOME A SIGNIFICANT RECREATIONAL RESOURCE FOR BOTH RESIDENTS AND VISITORS OF SALT LAKE CITY. BONNEVILLE SHORELINE TRAIL - ANOTHER SIGNIFICANT AND ONGOING ADVOCACY EFFORT CONDUCTED BY TRAILS UTAH INVOLVED THE CENTRAL WASATCH NATIONAL CONSERVATION AND RECREATION AREA LEGISLATION. IN THIS BILL, SPONSORED AND INTRODUCED BY JASON CHAFFETZ, UTAH'S CONGRESSMAN FROM THE 2ND DISTRICT IN 2016, NEW WILDERNESS IN THE WASATCH MOUNTAINS IS TO BE CREATED AND EXISTING WILDERNESS BOUNDARIES ARE TO BE AMENDED TO ALLOW FOR A SHARED-USE BONNEVILLE SHORELINE TRAIL (BST). THE BST, PLANNED AND EMBRACED BY COMMUNITIES AROUND THE SALT LAKE VALLEY AND BEYOND, WAS ENVISIONED AS A NON-MOTORIZED URBAN-INTERFACE TRAIL AVAILABLE TO FOOT TRAFFIC AND MOUNTAIN BIKERS LINKING NEIGHBORHOODS TOGETHER THROUGHOUT NORTHERN UTAH. TRAILS UTAH, THROUGH STUDY AND FIELD WORK, IDENTIFIED RETRACTIONS DESCRIBED IN THE BILL COULD NOT, IN FACT, SUPPORT A SHARED USE TRAIL BECAUSE OF GEOGRAPHIC AND PRIVATE PROPERTY CONSTRAINTS. WE SUBMITTED OUR FINDINGS IN TESTIMONY ON THE BILL TO THE HOUSE RESOURCES COMMITTEE AND HAD TO OPPOSE THE BILL IN ITS CURRENT FORM. WE HAVE SINCE JOINED A COALITION WITH OTHER TRAIL ORGANIZATIONS, CONSERVATION ORGANIZATIONS, THE FOREST SERVICE, AND OTHER STAKEHOLDERS TO MAKE SURE THAT WHEN THE BILL IS RE-INTRODUCED IT CONTAINS WILDERNESS BOUNDARY RETRACTIONS THAT CAN ADEQUATELY ACCOMMODATE BOTH HIKERS AND BIKERS ALONG THE BST.

name: SEED FARM
mission: Farm Business Incubator: The Seed Farm's farm business incubator provided new farmers with access to land, equipment, infrastructure, mentoring, market opportunities, and more, at reduced rates. During the 2017 growing season, six new farmers received access to these critical and often cost-prohibitive resources. This access allowed them to launch and grow their businesses, receiving intensive support during the risky and expensive first few years of farm ownership. While at The Seed Farm, new farmers receive ongoing instruction on environmentally sustainable growing practices, build credit and a customer base, and lay a solid foundation for their new farms. Incubator farmers must submit annual reports, sharing their income and expenses, challenges and successes from the past year, to The Seed Farm's program committee for review and feedback from experienced growers and educators. Two incubator farms operated on site in 2017. Four new farmers who farmed elsewhere in the Lehigh Valley benefited from "a la carte" access to incubator resources, such as space in the greenhouse and the use of tractors and implements, at reduced rates.; New Farmer Training: Most new farmers who come from non-farming backgrounds lack vital knowledge and training in many skills that are critical for long-term farming success. The Seed Farm has identified 122 critical knowledge and skill areas, including production, marketing, business planning, and equipment operation. In 2017, new farmer training was delivered in a skills-focused, "short course" format that offered a combination of hands-on experience and classroom instruction. This model was tailored to the needs of beginning farmers due to its increased accessibility and decreased cost. 32 beginning farmers from urban farms and community gardens participated in the short course, Vegetable Farming Basics. Course participants gained hands-on experience and learned the skills critical to producing specialty crops on a commercial scale. Three new farmers completed the course, Introduction to Tractor Operation, in which they gained tractor operating experience as well as more formal lessons on operation and safety. Our new CSA Workshare program allowed 15 community members to gain farming experience and work one-on-one with skilled Seed Farm staff for three hours per week, in exchange for a box of farm-fresh vegetables and herbs. And our newly-launched partnership with Community Bike Works brought six youths from center city Allentown to the farm once a week for four weeks during the summer, providing an introduction to farming as well as life skills, work skills, and increased access to fresh, local food.; Public farm-based education and outreach. The Seed Farm conducted guided farm visits, community programming, and farm-based workshops in 2017 to provide education on sustainable agriculture, the Lehigh Valley food system and farm operation. 499 community members increased their knowledge and skills by visiting our farm and participating in programming with our partners such as Penn State Extension, Pennsylvania FarmLink, Rodale Institute, and the PA Association for Sustainable Agriculture.
